In the *Vijayottaratantra*,
the chapter on the worship of Śiva states: "The ritual sacrifice (*iṣṭi*) for Śambhu, who is devoid of form, is prescribed as being universal."
If there is the relinquishing of royal wealth, there will be the absence of life in the eastern direction.
And that [power] is contemplated by Śiva at the tips of the prongs of the liṅga;
or else, the fire, consecrated by mantra, is the form of the Guru of the liṅga.
Together with Śiva, the Lord of Knowledge, he is free from the discrimination between Śiva and the object of knowledge;
he dwells in a state of constant stability, possessing equal affection for the Liṅga, the sacred fire, Śiva, and the Vidyā.
Whether it be a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*), a mandala, or another form with its own shape,
everything situated there is the irreproachable form of Śambhu.
O Śambhu, the meditation on the Head (mūrdhnikti) is of two kinds: with a witness (sākṣikā) and without a witness (nirākṣikā).
The other form is for those desiring specific fruits (kāmyā), while the supreme form consists of eternal consciousness.
Having thus determined one of the forms, such as the *liṅga* and so forth, the practitioner [should worship] Śiva, the Lord of embodied beings, whose body is known by others through that [form].
Every day, one should worship the Lord preceded by the five purifications:
the purification of the self, the place, the qualities, the materials, and the mantra.
The purifications are now described in sequence according to the procedure stated in the five mantras:
having performed the ritual bath with the Tantra-mantras, one who has washed his feet and hands is pure.
Having performed the placement of hand gestures and limbs, one should worship with the general *arghya* offering;
one should worship Gaṇeśa at the top, Bhāratī above him, and Lakṣmī in the center.
On the southern side of the door, one should worship Nandin and Gaṅgā;
elsewhere in the sanctuary, with perfumes, flowers, and auspicious unbroken rice grains.
Having entered with the left foot, one should then worship the limbs of the Vidyā and the weapons; then, having offered a seat in the center of the site for its Lord, one should proceed.
Having brought [the disciple] into the hand of Hara, one should unite him with that very form of Bhava within the pure Śiva, having meditated on the path and the cessation at the crown of the head.
By means of the heart-syllable ending in *saṃ*, within the self of Śiva that transcends Śiva,
by the all-pervading Lord whose senses are inflamed, or else within the solar orb.
Deprived of the heart-cave and the reflected image, he emits from the power of his own radiance a self in the form of vital breath (prāṇa), resembling the rising sun.
Having first united with the Self, one should perform the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi).
This consists of the elements beginning with earth, the three states beginning with cessation (nivṛtti), the digits (kalās), the principles (tattvas), and so forth, arising from the support.
In the case of the arising of the five, one should purify [the mantra] up to the end of the "it" (i) by means of the *saṃhita* alone.
One should meditate upon the earth, which has attained purity by itself and possesses the nature of water resembling milk;
its navel is marked by a seed-syllable, shining like a lotus and resembling a crescent moon.

Having purified that which stands within the *la* with the *śikhā*, one performs four rounds of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*). Having thus purified the *pratiṣṭhā*, one purifies the fire from the feet up to the ears.
One should know that the three-pointed [figure] is the form of the Svastika, which is long according to other traditions of knowledge.
When there is an elevation of prosperity, one should subsequently cast the wind [element] with three [units] above the eyebrows.
One should purify the six-pointed star and the dot (bindu) within the six-faced [deity], which is indeed black;
for the sake of purification, the [mantras] beginning with Nivṛtti and ending with *Huṃ Phaṭ* should be applied.
Then, one should purify with the Astra-mantra the body of the Vyomatantra, which is pervasive and designated as the Bindu, resembling pure crystal and circular in shape.
The weapon is said to be the Śivāstra alone, and not any other Pāśupata weapon;
likewise, through the purification of the kalās and so forth, all bonds are completely cleansed.
One should contemplate the form with a form consisting of the *praṇava*, which is of the nature of the Self;
having brought that [form] near, one should then contemplate it as the immortal Self.
With the root mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ*, one should contemplate the seat of Śiva in the center;
there, having visualized the form, one should install the Brahmāṇīs starting from the thumb.
Having clearly distinguished the forms of Rudra and the others, one should perform the ritual of the mantra-body;
having bestowed the eye and invoked [the deity], one should install Śiva and his limbs.
Having again placed Śiva at the end of the little finger for the sake of supreme action, and having encircled [the hand] with the *vaṃ* syllable on the thumb, one should employ it in all rites.
Then one should perform the deposition of the body (dehanyāsa) together with the mudrās as it is taught:
[placing] Īśa, Tatpuruṣa, Aghora, Guhyaka, Jāta, and Śambara.
One should perform the sacrifice known as Brahmavaktra and install Ālāla and Lobha in the faces, starting from the mouth, heart, secret place, genitals, and the pair of thighs and knees.
One should worship Īśāna with the mantra *parimūrdhā*, the faces with the *puruṣa* mantra,
the two ears and shoulders with the *dvyaṅguri* mantra, and the navel, belly, and lower torso with the *avara* mantra.
The knower of mantras, using the Aghora mantra in its eightfold form (*vasurūpa*), should fashion [the image]:
the secret organ, the linga, the elephant, the knee, the two shanks, and the hips.
And on the side, the practitioner of mantras, while recollecting the Vāmadeva mantra, should assign [the syllables] to the feet,
the palms of the hands, the nose, the head, the arms, the thighs, and the knees.
Having thus recollected the body of Vidyā, Śiva should then place that [mantra];
afterwards, he should place the limbs of Śiva, beginning with the Heart, upon the [corresponding] locations beginning with the heart.
The practitioner should place heart upon heart and head upon head;
having placed crest upon crest, he should then assign the armor to all the limbs.
One should first abandon the weapon [mantra] abiding on the palms of one's own hands;
then, one should perform the internal sacrifice within the heart with devotion and meditative states.
Having mentally prepared the seat, one should then invoke the two forms of Śiva;
having invoked Śiva along with his attendants, one should offer the water for the guest-offering (arghya), the water for washing the feet (pādya), and so forth.
With the consecrations of the five nectars and so forth, with the anointing of divine perfumes,
and with various garments such as fine silk and cotton cloths for the body;
One should worship the deity along with his attendants externally with flowers made of gold and red minerals, incense, lamps, sacred threads, and various kinds of food offerings.
Having thus performed the *nāsti-nyāsa*, one should manifest the perfected state in heaven;
[the drops] flow unimpeded from the *bindu* as pure, auspicious nectars.
O Śiva, one should meditate upon the incense and the lamp as being within the *bindu* together with the *ahaṃ*.
Having done this, one should perform the purification of the locus for that which resides within.
The base is of three kinds, sequentially encased by armor.
Then, having brought the arghya vessel and washed it with water using the Astra-mantra:

Having prepared the *arghya* offering with flowers, rice, white mustard, barley, *darbha* grass, barley, and sesame seeds, consecrated with the *saṃhitā-mantra* and rendered immortal by the *surabhī-mantra*.
The water is nectar, and its support is the power Kuṇḍalinī;
for the sake of establishing its modifications and so forth, there are the terms "support of nectar," "the earth," and others.
The *arghya* offering is distinguished by that through which Śambhu is propitiated;
having sprinkled the ritual materials with that [water], one should consecrate them with the *hṛdaya-mantra* and the *śara-mantra*.
Having performed the ritual bath and worshiped equally, one should perform the purification of the mantra by reciting eleven mantras beginning with "Oṃ" and ending with "Namaḥ."

Having reached the harsh words [of the mantra] according to the sequence of days, one who possesses the subtle *liṅga* should cause the recitation of the *Gāyatrī* and the ancient worship with a common *arghya*.
One should wash the liṅga together with its pedestal using the Astra-mantra until it is stainless;
then, one should prepare its seat according to the prescribed rule, as that procedure is ordained.
First, one should establish Śakti, who is the form of all supports, with the heart-mantra;
likewise, having restrained Nanda with the heart-mantra, [one should contemplate] knowledge and the perfection of dispassion.
When the reversal from the fire [element] occurs, one should fashion the limbs;
through the power of *māyā* and *vidyā*, one manifests them together with the pericarp of the lotus.
O Lord, one should mentally conceive the omnipresent Deity as consisting of five seats: Vāmā and the other Śaktis, the orbs of the Sun, Moon, and Fire, and the enemy of the lord (Śiva).
One should contemplate the feet as white, red, yellow, and black;
the various colors of the limbs [should be visualized] with the left side as red and pale-white.
An eight-petalled white lotus with a yellow-colored pericarp;
the Śaktis are like the sun, and the ninth is like the rising of crystal.
In this manner, one should install the form of the All-pervasive Lord upon the seat of yoga;
one should place the Heart-mantra, encapsulated by the Sadyojāta mantra, within the form that is beyond the range of the senses.

One should perform the ritual identification (*sakalīkaraṇa*) with the six Brahmans, who are red, consist of four forms, and are endowed with the *kalā* beyond tranquility (*śāntyatīta*), their eyes being like grains of rice.
This is the body of knowledge (vidyātanu) of Śambhu, consisting of his own power and instruments;
having placed that body of knowledge within the range of the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra).
Resembling pure crystal, he has five faces and three eyes;
he possesses ten arms and is endowed with five matted locks that are slightly reddish.
[The right hands hold] a sword, a trident, a spear, [the gestures of] grace, fearlessness, and honor; [and the left hands hold] a serpent, a rosary, a lotus, a mango fruit, and a water-pot.
The face of Īśāna was brilliantly white, the face of Puru was the color of saffron,
the southern face was formidable, and the northern face was radiant.
Having thus meditated upon the supreme breast of Śambhu, which possesses all forms and is characterized by sixteen years of age, [located] from the western face of the Ocean of Milk.
In that [vessel], one should invoke the upward-moving path of the serpents;
with a full handful of flowers, the mind is withdrawn from other objects into the Kumbha.
Having ejected [the breath] together with the letter *i*,
[one perceives it] within the range extending from the heart, throat, palate, and the aperture between the eyebrows up to the *bindu*,
appearing like [a flame of] fire.
Having entered the Sadyojāta mantra, she enters the path of Brahman;
with throbbing red channels, she reaches the proximity of the Peak-syllable (kūṭa) at the forehead.
In the battle of the downward breath (apāna), this vehicle with two doors has emerged along a path filled with blazing rays.

One should place the flower that has been in the water upon the image, and with the heart-mantra, establish Śiva in union with the heart; one should then perform the rites of presence (sannidhi) and firm fixation (sannirodha), and assign the limbs (aṅga) beginning with the heart.
One should perform the practice of Mahāmudrā according to the ritual procedure with the root mantra;
thus, the wise should [perform] Mahāmudrā through the rites of invocation and so forth.
One should prepare the locus for sacrifice by purifying the Lord with the six purificatory rites (saṃskāras);
therein, having abandoned the rungs beginning with Brahmā, one should proceed as the self of Śiva.
The path beyond the serpent is within this drop; there is the birth of the imperishable.
Having struck it in the city, there is the installation of the All-pervasive Lord.
For one who has been consecrated and is seated, that which constitutes the acceptance of various things through the waters of discipline from his own servants is the very presence of the Lord.
The proximity of this [mantra] is its cessation; thus it is explained by virtue of its power.
It cannot be overcome by the [deities] beginning with Hṛdaya and ending with Astra, even when they are empowered by their respective mantras.

My [teaching] has been proclaimed as all-pervading; because it effects the liberation from the state of being a bound soul (paśutva) and the attainment of the state of Śiva, and because it causes the removal of the individual soul (aṇu).
(8) Among those endowed with the meaning of the two syllables, she increases the delight in the mudrās;
therefore, at the conclusion of the ritual action, she bestows grace upon the universe.
O Lord, you have attained all that is to be attained;
even the Tathāgata has been surpassed by me in this regard.
Then, remembering him whose face was radiant with joy and whose every limb was beautiful,
he offered him a vessel, as well as water for washing the feet and water for sipping.
O Lord, having performed the rite called *kara-sammukha* with the offering of clarified butter,
one should then fumigate Śambhu with *dūrvā* grass, flowers, and unbroken grains (*akṣata*).

Having bathed [the deity] extensively with the five nectars of cow-products and so forth, it should be performed according to the procedure interspersed with the offering of flowers, incense, and water for honor (*arghya*).
Having dried the body with dehydrating substances such as ground āmalaka and turmeric,
one should wash it with pure water and finally with scented water.
Having smeared Dhūrjaṭi with a paste of moon-fragrance, sandalwood, and saffron,
and having clothed Soma in garments such as fine silk and linen;
She is said to be adorned with ornaments such as a crown; release her even by various methods, having assigned the collection of Brahma’s limbs to their respective places upon the body of the Lord.
Having offered the desired incense and the *ārātrī* lamp, and having given the water for rinsing (*camana*) and the *arghya* offering,
one should present the oblation (*haviḥ*) to the Lord with the *samudgama* and *brahma* mantras.
Then, after the offering of betel leaves, one should cast the *bali* offering to the Kanyās and others;
afterwards, having worshipped the enclosures (*āvṛti*) and the limbs (*aṅga*) of Brahmāṇī with permission.
Having gathered [the substances] from their respective places, one should worship them with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, in the center,
in the east and other directions, and ending with the northwest, northeast, south, and west.
One should worship the weapon-mantra according to the rules at the tips of the petals in the four directions;
then, having offered incense that has been sprinkled with water and honored with the heart-mantra.
The *ārātrika* ceremony was performed, and lamps were arranged all around.
Having applied a protective mark (tilaka) on their foreheads with ashes that destroys demons,
[he presented] a mirror, a fly-whisk, a parasol, and whatever else was auspicious.
First, one should offer [the oblation] to Śiva with the heart-mantra amidst auspicious sounds such as musical instruments;
at the conclusion of the offering of the *ārātrika*, the *nīrājana* rite is performed at night.
The ritual procedure for that [fire] is now being stated here incidentally:
either in the kitchen or elsewhere, upon a circle made of cow dung.
Having placed there bowls made of gold, silver, and so forth, and having washed them,
one should place the fire within them, from the center of the sacrificial pit up to Īśvara.
Otherwise, O Brahmin, he should not enter;
then, having anointed those wicks with ghee, he should place them [in the lamps] along with auspicious items such as cow dung and the like.
Having had it carried by women or by male attendants,
one should draw a mandala before Śiva, with the two auspicious ones (Umā and Śiva) in its center.
Having sprinkled nine, five, or even one heap of lamps with the weapon-mantra and the *arghya* water, one should worship them up to the incense offering with the heart-mantra.
Lamps produced from the common source have been gathered; then, having drawn them forth from the fire arisen at the navel, one should join and deposit them.
Having led [the breath] through the *pūraka* and *kumbhaka*, one should perform the fivefold [breath-control] beginning with *sadyojāta* and so forth,
and then cause the Lord to revolve by means of the previously mentioned consecrations.
(On page 10:
Whether in three ways, three times, or even once, [he should do so] as if delighted with salt and other substances.
Then, at the conclusion of the offering of ashes, he should cast [the remains] outside, ending with the lamps.
In that very place, one should perform the daily fire-oblation (nityahoma) with sacrificial fuel (samidh) and other materials,
using vessels made of gold, silver, and so forth, which have the appearance of a tripod (yantrikā).

Through the chapter on food offerings, one attains perfection; therefore, one should present various kinds of food offerings, along with specific accessories, to the trident-bearer who is accompanied by his consort.
Having given water separately, sandalwood for the one with arms raised like bellows,
and betel-leaf joined with camphor, one should cause [these] to be offered to Caṇḍa.
Then, one should offer the *bali* to the attendants, such as Nandin and others,
either all around or where they are situated outside as the outer limbs of the retinue.
Then, at the conclusion of the offering of oblations, one should perform the removal of the food offering (naivedya) and other rites,
as well as present dūrvā grass, flowers, unbroken rice grains (akṣata), and the sacrificial thread (yajñasūtra) to the Supreme Lord.
Having offered a golden garment and cotton, while reciting the root mantra,
one should invoke Śiva as before and present incense and the ārātrika lamp.

Having recited [the mantra] according to one's capacity with the heart-mantra, one should offer [the water] even in secret with words beginning with "guhya," using fragrant water according to the rite, while protecting it with the weapon and armor mantras.
One should please the Supreme Lord with songs, dances, hymns, and praises, with auspicious sounds such as "Victory!", and with prostrations, eulogies, and the like.
Then, having gained knowledge for the sake of the fire-oblation, he should go to the place where the fire is maintained;
and having offered there according to the rule, beginning with the oblation and ending with the sipping of water.
Having performed the placement of the limbs and hands, one should offer the fire-oblation (homa);
and having caused the daily festival and the *tāṇḍava* dance to be performed according to the rule.
With the hand turned away, as if always bestowing [offerings] upon the heads,
having offered the *arghya* and raised the limbs by means of the application of the *heti-mudrā*.
Then, one should withdraw the network of limbs from Śambhu’s abode,
while constantly maintaining the expectation of dismissal within the remaining lingas.
Furthermore, by the offering of the arghya, there is also the withdrawal of Śiva;
this [rite] should always be performed independently upon the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) and other such sites.
When the indifferent Śiva has been abandoned, purification of the *liṅga* is prescribed;
otherwise, the floral offerings and so forth remain on the *liṅga* as *nirmālya*.
One should worship the deity in the image either at the four junctions of the day,
or else in the forenoon, midday, morning, evening, and at the end of the night.

Whether in the forenoon, at midday, or in the afternoon—or indeed during both the forenoon and midday—one who is self-restrained should worship the Lord; for then, O Haṃsa, one attains the supreme goal.
The Aṣṭapuṣpikā begins with the offering of flowers and ends with the ritual bath;
it is called "a mere fragment" when one is unable or of inferior conduct to perform it fully.
Then, the seat of Śiva, the image, the root mantra, and the five limbs;
by the offering of these to those born [of the lineage], there shall be the eightfold flower-offering (aṣṭapuṣpikā) to Śiva.
The ritual with the eight flowers does not conclude with sound;
at the end of the day, one should worship the Lord of the gods together with the Goddess.
Having extensively adorned it on all sides with abundant perfumes, flowers, and the like, as well as with side-dishes such as cakes, and with flower garlands.
At the conclusion of the worship, having daily honored one's own guru with perfumes, flowers,
and sacred threads with devotion, one should [request] the boon for the procedure of one's chosen *liṅga*.
One's own chosen *liṅga* is for oneself, while another may be chosen even among those of others;
one's own chosen [liṅga] bestows its fruit upon oneself, whereas another brings about a different fruit.
Whether they be Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, or Śūdras, as well as their wives,
and those with hair growing in the natural direction (anuloma), they are all entitled to perform sacrifices according to their own desires using gold and other materials.
Furthermore, for other venerable objects as well, circumambulation is performed swiftly;
or else, one may perform worship at a common linga, but no one of another caste [should do so].
When the signs are common, one who knows the nature of the Lord of the Samaya should then worship there that [deity] whose form consists of supreme grace.
Then, the practitioner who has been consecrated or initiated is fit for the worship of Sāraṇā,
being devoted to the Śiva-tattva and the other principles.

This eternal worship of Śiva, consisting of all mantras, is enjoined as being characterized by one's own chosen *liṅga*, by the daily rite, and by the festival rite, even when the former two have perished.
His entry into all tantras remains for the sake of Śaṅkara;
it must be guarded with effort by those who have not yet emerged from the [inner] sacrifice.
Henceforth, the procedure for the fire-ritual is prescribed in brief.
Thus ends the chapter on the worship of Śiva in the *Vijayottara*, the compendium of three thousand verses.
The Ritual Procedure for Worshiping the Serpents:
Now, the sacrifice for the worship of the serpents, performed for the sake of one's desires, is prescribed.
One should have a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) constructed in the southeast, either circular or square.
An elephant-girth belt adorned with a cord and further embellished by a yoni;
the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) is one cubit in length and two, three, or four finger-breadths in height.
The girdle and its cord are situated outside the measurement of the ear;
the water-pot (kuṇḍikā) is considered to be of that same dimension and similar in width.

From the measure of two cubits up to the maximum limit, when divided by three, eight, or five, the resulting portion is to be known as the *aṅgula*; from that, one should determine the girdle (*mekhalā*).
The width should be eight finger-breadths (aṅgulas) and the length twelve finger-breadths;
for elephants, the yoni should be made similar [in size], or it should be placed in proximity to the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa).
The half-circle of Karṇapāda-vṛtta, extending fifty units forward and backward, shall indeed be the Yoni-kuṇḍa; it is the union of two yonis.
The portion of Vasu (eight) from the tree (five), increased by Śambhu (eleven), Krodha (sixteen), and the moon (one);
with the increase of three parts from Matsya (four), the night-stalker (Rāhu) becomes three.
A circle drawn with a radius increased by one-tenth [of its diameter] grants all desires;
when increased by one-sixth, it forms a fish, an arrow, a trident, a goad, or a lotus.
The lotus, with a girdle of lotus-like luster, stands firm in its crushing and punishing [of obstacles];
it is the source of the limbs of Gāyatrī, arising from the ear of the Radiant One.
For those who desire [the fruits of] the ritual, the sacrificial ground (*yaṣṭa*) should extend to the ears and be covered with cloth;
or, in its absence, it should be a bare patch of earth (*sthaṇḍila*) or a circle made of cow dung.
Having accomplished [the rite] with the *lokyadūla* weapon, having sprinkled it with the *varma* [mantra],
and having consecrated it with the *astra* [mantra], one should cause it to tremble by means of digging, uprooting, and filling.
Likewise, the leveling and sprinkling, as well as the pounding and the *pārjara*,
the plastering, the construction of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), and the encircling and worship;
Three lines facing east, drawn with a sharp-pointed [instrument] by Rudra or Īśa,
should be made into a vajra upon the bee and other [elements] with the sword of meditation.
Then, having prepared a seat with a lamp placed in its center, one should proceed.

The practitioner of mantra should worship that [deity] in the center with the heart-mantra, O Lord; likewise, the master of speech should worship the Lord of Remembrance and the others, or the one born of that yoga, in the middle or at the opening of the nose.
One should cast [the seed] into her womb who is fit for conception; having abandoned the portion of the liquor, one should approach the triad of fires, or else observe the subsequent signs therein.
Having obtained the mantra-saṃhitā, having made [the offering] nectar through the *dhenu-mudrā*,
and having performed the rite of enrichment (*pūrjita*), one should perform it three times over the *yama-kuṇḍa*.
Then,
having worshipped with the Sadyojāta mantra for the sake of conception, one should offer oblations of clarified butter while casting the semen along with the ritual substance into the fire.
One should worship with the *puṃs* mantra and offer oblations with the head-mantra (*śiras*) and the heart-mantra (*hṛd*).
One should perform the oblation with the *iṣvāva-uṣas* mantra and the crest-mantra (*śikhā*) in rites for prosperity.
And with that [mudrā], one should arrange the limbs of the sacrificial arena on the *darbha* grass before the fire;
having performed the acts of cutting and opening, the rite of generating the fire (*agnerjanana*) follows.
Then the wise man, remembering Śiva, should kindle the fire with his own [mantra];
he should offer three oblations of sesame seeds with the *nṛ-nṛ* mantra and the *ātmatantra*.
Then, for the destruction of the birth-impurity (sūtaka), one should sprinkle the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) with arghya water;
having strewn darbha grass around it, one should not sit down nor bring the sacrificial animal (ālāla).
Having performed this once, one should offer five fuel-sticks and likewise five more;
upon them, one should place the seats for Brahmā, Rudra, Acyuta, and Īśvara.

One should employ the Lords of the World (lokeśas) upon the girdles for the purpose of protection; having worshipped the lords of the directions (īśānānām) for the sake of their respective functions, one should offer oblations with the weapon-mantra (astra).
Then one should give a name to the fire, saying, "You are Śivāgni";
thereafter, the purification of the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles must be performed for the sacrificial rite.
The *sruk* and *sruva* ladles should be made of *vaikaṅkata* wood, or else from a sacrificial tree;
they should be one cubit in length and have mouths fashioned with the coils of a serpent.
Though having one ear, it is also said to have two; it possesses two morae and is fourfold.
On the banks of the Daṇḍyā, however, it is adorned with four *kalaśas* and twice seven [syllables].
Or six [petals] of two mātrās each, adorned with circles of ghee and lotuses,
provided with hands possessing back-petals and lips, and circular in shape.
The outlets for the clarified butter (ājya) should be the size of the little finger;
having fixed the handle of the ladle (sruva), its length should be thirty-six parts of the smallest measure.
Its length is also measured by those same eighteen finger-breadths;
its ritual function is that of a thumb-sized [implement], and it has a lotus-shaped base.
It has two tiers in front, while elsewhere it resembles the head of an elephant.
One should pull out the root with sharp strokes; it must not be left unstruck.
It should be made thin down to the base, like a reed stalk from its sheath.
Those who always desire the fruit of all things should fashion the bases of the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles;
I, the Lord of Horses, declare that the *vimāna* (pedestal) is common to all *tantras*.
The *sruk* is the power (*śakti*) whose form is action, while the *sruva* is Maheśvara himself;
therefore, the two oblations (*homa*) are performed with these two, which possess auspicious characteristics.
Having performed this, one should wash the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles with water;
then, having whirled them over the fire, one should pass them in front, through the middle, and across the sacrificial grass (*barhis*).
Having touched all [the parts] with the root-mantra using one's whole being,
and having placed the triple-sectioned [seat], one should worship Śiva and Śakti within those two.
Then, having brought cow's milk placed in a good vessel and purified with a cloth,
one should heat it over the fire until it boils and bring it to the point of overflowing.
A true purifier consists of two long tips knotted together at the middle;
it should be held with the ring finger and thumb joined, facing toward the fire.
In that same manner, one should [place] it three times with the mantra, facing oneself,
and likewise three times with the heart-mantra, facing oneself.
Then one should place the tips of darbha grass, a span in length, into the midst of the clarified butter;
having performed the lustration (*nīrājana*) with the *ud-iti* verses, one should meditate upon the deity for the sake of the oblation.
In the middle [of the altar], he should offer to Agni; then, on the second square from the northeast, he should offer to Soma.
Furthermore, the Guru should offer to Agni-Sviṣṭakṛt during the bright fortnight.
Otherwise, however, having offered to Soma, one should offer to Ravi;
when this is done, it becomes the "Flame of Fire" (Vahni-śikhā) for rites dedicated to Śiva.
Auspicious rites should never be performed for one who is not Śiva;
for that reason, Śiva must be employed as the fire-god in the ritual action.
Its activity proceeds even beyond other saṃskāras;
the Śivāgama, having pierced through the five saṃskāras beginning with *garbhādhāna*, [bestows liberation].
Consecrations that have been accomplished by means of the three fires do not lead to success at all when performed again for rites such as malevolent magic (*abhicāra*).

Otherwise, if one performs the consecration for the sake of attaining supernatural powers (*siddhi*) upon the sacrificial leaf or within oneself, that person, through lack of discernment, destroys those very powers.
The fire-oblation for those called Śaivas is said to be performed in the Śiva-fire;
for others, it has been previously described there as being of the nature of Śiva within the Śiva-fire.
Indeed, the mantras prescribed for the various ritual acts in the Vedic tradition,
when employed in the fire of Śiva, make the performer a vessel for the oblation.

At this juncture, it should be stated that the offering of *havya* and *kavya* and so forth is performed upon the *loṭa*; the definitive conclusion of the scriptural meaning is that the *homa* is offered within Śivāśrita.
He who, in the absence of a fire, performs the purificatory rites for the embryo and so forth with fire produced by friction—
since the Gāyatrī is the warder-off [of evil]— from him such a son is born.
The fire, which arises from the end of the *śrīkaṇṭha* mantra and so forth, would be without mantras;
its consecration (*saṃskāra*) must be performed through the five embryos (*pañcagarbha*) in due order.
When the Śivāgni has been thus accomplished, one should deposit the fire of consumption [into it];
having brought the two forms, consisting of the manifest and the unmanifest, into that fire.
There, furthermore, one should offer oblations as before for Śiva, or for another deity accompanied by the presiding deities (varaṇa),
using fuel-sticks, clarified butter, sesame seeds, rice, barley, and so forth.
O best of charioteers, you may perform the fire-offering (homa) as you desire;
however, in the absence of clarified butter, the offering should be made with sesame seeds and black mustard.

In the portion dedicated to Śiva, one should perform the oblation for the limbs and for the Brahman-priests as well; having thus offered with their respective mantras, the final offering of water for the messengers follows.
Having performed the consultation, one should then dismiss the auspicious ash as before;
one should always protect the fire by means of the oblation of the four *vyāhṛtis*.
Alternatively, one may dismiss the fire and, having performed the consecration again, rejoin it;
the daily consecration of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) is preceded by the removal of the ashes.
Then, having prepared a mandala and worshipped Rudra and the others in due order with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, one should likewise satisfy them with offerings.
The Rudras are stationed in the east, the Mothers in the south, and the Gaṇas in the west;
all the planets are in the north, and the seven-flamed deity (Agni) is situated among the gods.
In the northeast are Pālāśī, Indra, Vāyu, the Nāgas, the lunar mansions, and the zodiac signs;
likewise, Viśvā, the Wind, and the Guardian of the Field (Kṣetrapa) are in the south.
Just as one who is pure, having remained in his place and satisfied the fire with offerings,
should withdraw it and return to the presence of Śiva carrying the vessel of sacrificial remains (arghya).
Furthermore, having offered the eightfold ritual action once to Śiva, one should dismiss the Lord there; the procedure for that has been stated previously.
Having dismissed the god Agni, who stood in the center previously,
she then entered the final linga situated in the middle for the sake of the omen.
Having offered the *prajāhuti* at night, the worship of Śiva is performed;
having offered the *gīr-huti* at the dwelling of the night-walker, the worship of Śiva is performed.
The Blessed Lord Śiva has declared that the night is for the residence [of the deity] and worship;
once this fire-rite is completed, the procedure for the daily festival should be performed.
The entire sequence of propitiation.
Now I shall explain in detail the sequence for the worship of the Sakala [deity];
that is proclaimed to be twofold: the primary [form] and the subsidiary limb.
The second [type] consists of those joined with the *gharivāra* and those devoid of it;
furthermore, that [second type] should be known as twofold according to the distinction of the Malaya mountain.
The image (bera) is said to be made of moving metal, or stone, or gems;
it may also be painted on cloth and the like, or fashioned from clay or wood.
This very thing remains as its function, devoid of a painted cloth;
for a mountain, though lacking painting, is mobile, whereas if it were possessed of painting, it would be stable.
The worshipful offering (argha) is threefold: the painted, the variegated, and likewise the reflected image.
A painting is seen as having all its parts visible, yet it lacks the perception of the tips of *darbha* grass;
it is devoid of depressions and elevations, being merely a fabricated representation such as a cloth or a mural.
That which is called Citrabhāsa is divine; likewise, when all that is joined with the variegated (citra) is worshipped together with the ritual worship (karmārca) among the Mothers.
Whether it be a jeweled liṅga, a pedestal, a form, or a mirror, these should be employed according to one's ritual capacity; or else, there may simply be a consecrated sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila).
At the base, the height of the *bera* (the main image) is established; then, dividing that by two, nine [units] are prescribed.
It is proclaimed as being of nine types according to the distinctions of *uttama* (superior) and so forth.
The vessel may be made from even three measures, or five, up to ten finger-breadths;
the measurement from the soles of the feet to the crown of the head is considered to be twelvefold.

Having divided the area for the door into nine parts, one should determine the measurement of the sanctum (dhāma) and its components, such as the base (bhāga), the plinth (bhaṇi), and the upper molding (uttara),
according to the ninefold measurement desired, or indeed the very meaning of the term "sanctum" itself.

Having fashioned the excellent form of the primary image (mūlabera) with the crescent moon as its crest, endowed with the six auspicious qualities beginning with longevity (āyus), and measured by you in digits (aṅgula) according to the proportions (aṃśas);
Or else, having obtained [the rite] from Somāskandeśvara by means of the patron,
one should perform it for the Lord exactly as before, including the independent, pure dance-gestures up to the offering of food (naivedya).
Having completed the daily rites such as bathing and so forth, one should enter the outer pavilion;
there, seated comfortably on pure ground, one should place the feet and the face [in their proper positions].
Having again performed the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi) and contemplated the divine body,
and having bathed it with streams of nectar, one should perform the internal sacrifice (antaryāga).

Then one should perform purification by bathing, and fashion a protective enclosure with the *astra* mantra; thereafter, having enveloped [the site] with the *kavaca* mantra, one should also prepare the sacrificial altar (*vedikā*).
Afterwards, one should purify the substances intended for worship;
having sprinkled them with the water of the general *arghya*, the practitioner, empowered by the mantra for all purposes, should touch them.
Then the mantra-master should purify them with the mantra beginning with *oṃ* and ending with *namaḥ*.
Having once attained the end of sound, one takes refuge in the pure reality.
O Hira, having prepared the general *arghya* offering consisting of perfumes, flowers, and unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*),
one should then arrange the water for washing the feet (*pādya*) and the other offerings in their proper sequence.

In a vessel made of gold, silver, or the like, or a conch shell belonging to the Lord of the Three-eyed One (Śiva), which has been washed with water containing *hetī* [mantras], it is then filled with water three times.

Having prepared water for the feet (pādya) consisting of sandalwood mixed with blood, or even flowers and water, one should offer it to the two feet while reciting the Sadyojāta mantra, and [offer] fire [to the feet] with the same.
The wise practitioner, having consecrated his mouth with the mouth-mantra, should prepare a mouth-cleansing rinse consisting of cloves, nutmeg, camphor, jasmine flowers, and cardamom fruits.
The *arghya* offering consists of milk, rice, white mustard seeds, the tips of *kuśa* grass, realgar (*manaḥśilā*), and *yavakṣāra*, combined with fragrance and flowers alone.
Having prepared it with the *saṃhitā* mantras and protected it with the *kavaca*,
one should cause the milk to shine forth with the *mudrā*, appearing like the very essence of milk.
Alternatively, having consecrated the vardhanī vessel,
the wise one, awakened by the Caṇḍamudrā, should sprinkle the doorway with the water from the arghya vessel.
One should always worship the door-keepers together with the sounds of bells:
Tigarbhā on the right door-jamb and [Tighaṇṭā] on the left.
And [he saw] Kālī, the daughter of Kalīga; and above Ga, Sarasvatī, who resembles Nandin and Śyāma, three-eyed and adorned with four staffs.
In the two hands, left and right, [he displays] the gesture of fearlessness and the pure mudrā;
on the left, the fingers are held in the boon-granting (varada) pose, or else he holds an antora lance.
Kālī has the luster of the color of saffron; she holds a noose and a goad in her hands, and possesses two excellent hands joined with the lord of the Nandī-bull.
Both [hands] on the palm of the left hand are joined with ashes;
they are endowed with matted locks, accompanied by serpents, and wear the sacrificial thread.
One should contemplate Nandi and Kāla with mouths formidable with fangs;
or, if they are endowed with two arms, the wise one should visualize them as previously described.
Red in color, with four arms, an elephant face, and his own tusk; holding a noose and an axe, adorned with a garland of human heads, and possessing three eyes smeared with ashes.
Vāgīśa has the luster of white color, four hands, and three eyes;
he holds a book, a rosary, and a water-pot.
With serene faces and adorned with crowns of matted hair, they hold [the weapons].
One should worship these gatekeepers with perfumes and other offerings by their respective names.

One should dispel the obstacles situated in the heavens, the atmosphere, and on the earth by means of the *puṣṭi-puṣṭa* foot-bindings and the weapon-mantra (*astra*), having removed them from the left branch.
Having entered the inner sanctum (garbhageha) and having fixed the weapon-mantras at the doors,
one should scatter parched grain (mahāpyarṇān) for the purpose of driving away obstacles.
The wise man should cast a curtain at that time over the nihilist who has been rubbed by those of contrary conduct, so as to prevent him from being seen.
Having fully worshipped Vāstoṣpati and the charioteer of the God of gods,
the preceptor prostrates himself like a staff upon the ground and makes a formal request for the worship.
Having performed the worship offered during the morning twilight with the Gāyatrī, the Marut,
taking a garland from the Brahmans, should present it to Caṇḍeśa.
If the first [vessel] is impure, one should purify it with servants and others using the *dhora-mantra*;
having purified it, one should [place] that deity [there] along with water for the *arghya* offering.
O Mantrin, one should never represent the head of the God as empty;
rather, one should depict the Śakti in the form of the support, with a luster white as cow’s milk.
One should then worship Nanda, who has four arms and three eyes, holding a noose, a goad, and displaying the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, seated upon a lotus throne that is the Veda.
Having ten arms and four faces, with a radiance like the jasmine flower or the moon,
he held a sword, a shield, a bow, arrows, a water-pot, and a sacred thread.
He is endowed with the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, holding a trident and a lotus in his hands;
he is the self of the lotus-throne, born from the ocean of the Śaktis and Buddhas.
One should meditate upon the beautiful lion-form, which possesses the knowledge of dharma, detachment, and sovereignty, whose feet are its limbs, and which is white like saffron and betel.
In the directions of Agni, Rakṣas, Marut, Sarpā, and Kaṣṭhā, one should likewise arrange them in reverse order; and from the east onwards, one should visualize the various colors of the limbs.

Thereafter, upon that altar, one should place [the syllables] resembling red and white [in color] in the directions of Nairṛti and Īśāna; then, having fixed the stalk, one should meditate upon the Destroyer.
Above that is a desired eight-petalled lotus, complete with a pericarp and filaments;
and upon the filaments are Vāmā and the others, possessing a radiance equal to ten million suns.
Likewise, one [form] has four arms, endowed with the lotus, the excellent [gesture], and the gesture of fearlessness;
facing her, he places Manonmanī upon the pericarp of the lotus at his front foot.
In the state of moonlight, one should contemplate the host of mandalas in their own essential form,
as well as the lords of the mandalas— the gods consisting of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Hara.
Then one should worship the upward-pervading power (śakti) whose nature is crooked;
the seat of Śiva is pervaded from [the level of] Vyādhi up to the end of Śuddhavidyā.
Before bathing, the wise one should worship with perfumes, flowers,
and incense the Goddess who has arisen from the three mandalas and whose nature is both manifest and unmanifest.
One should worship the embodied form of the Lord within the mantra;
the wise person should contemplate the body according to the specific deity.

The various forms of Śambhu, appearing in many ways according to their respective functions, constitute the limbs of renunciation (nyāsa) within the Brahman for one who has become Brahman under their own respective teacher.
Even though He is partless, they are seen to be dear for the sake of bestowing grace upon practitioners;
the restraint is by the Puruṣa alone, and the enveloping is by the Kavaca.
25) Afterwards, the Preceptor performs the *amṛtīkaraṇa* (the rite of immortalization) with the root mantra;
thus he worships the Supreme Lord, who is remembered as being purified by these consecrations (*saṃskāra*).
Just as the state [of the deity] is taught through ritual procedures when one is composed,
so too should the invocation and other rites for Somāskandeśvara be performed for those two.
The most excellent individual gurus, each with their own specific mantra,
should reverently offer betel-leaf and mouth-freshener with the *hṛdaya-mantra*.
Having diligently worshipped that deity in the center with the battle-offering (*raṇapūjā*),
and having worshipped the God together with Skanda and Umā on all sides;
The seat of Īśa is like Rudrākṣa; in the northeast, it is like saffron for a man;
in the south, the terrible one is like the *janu* fruit; and in the north, it should be like a flower.
One should contemplate [the deity] immediately in the west, pure as a moonbeam;
with one face and three eyes, and endowed with a crown of matted hair.
From the heart [to] the white heart in the southeast with the *hṛdaya* mantra;
then from the head [to] the golden-hued head in the northeast with the *śiras* mantra.
In the southwest, the auspicious limb and [the mantra] with a peak as red as the rising sun;
for all limbs, the black armor, and in the northwest, indeed by means of the armor.
One should worship the eye, which is tawny in color, by means of the station of Śiva;
it resembles the fire of the three times (hatrikālāgni) in the four directions beginning with the east.
Having thus worshipped the enclosure, one should again worship the site;
this includes the worship of the goddesses, those joined with Skanda and others, the *ceras*, and the limbs of the body, as well as the unobstructed worship of all.
One should perform either a bath or a sprinkling during the rite of daily worship;
however, for the occasional (naimittika) worship of the Lord, one should perform a ceremonial bath in pavilions and other such structures.
Having performed the rite of circumambulation accompanied by song, dance, and so forth,
[one should offer] pure oil, half-ash, *durvā* sprouts, and unbroken rice grains with the hands.
The essence characterized by flour, like impurities such as *malaka* and the like,
and even one deficient in caste— such as a Śūdra and so forth— one should imagine as being [like] flour and the like.
Having had fragrant garments, flowers, and other auspicious items carried by Brahmins and others, accompanied by the sounding of conchs, trumpets, and other musical instruments, [he should proceed].
In a place suitable for the ritual bathing and other rites, the wise one should sprinkle the foremost of gods with water, bow down with the *namratī* mudrā, and perform the circumambulation.
Thereafter, provided with betel-leaf and mouth-fresheners,
he should place a stone before the deity, sprinkle it with water, and worship it with the weapon-mantra (hetimantra).

Having offered the beginning with oil and other substances, along with garments and flowers, [he places] a drop on the head of the deity; then, with dūrvā sprouts and unbroken rice grains, [he offers them] at the feet, the arms, and the head.
Afterwards, having extracted the essence of two other leaves from a flour-mound with water,
one should sprinkle the head of the deity with those auspicious waters.
Thereafter, at night, one should apply an ointment that has been interspersed with the offering of flowers;
then, one should perform the worship of the village, beginning slowly with the foremost deity.
One should apply color with diamonds and other gems, and offer parched grain and incense;
having wiped him with a clean cloth, he shall become a lord through this divine state.
Having offered clothing, ornaments, perfumes, garlands, incense, and lamps,
one should perform the auspicious *ārātrika* ceremony while reciting the *parivarta*.
There were fifty-seven lamp-bearers stationed on trays, some holding lamps in their hands,
others standing upon abundant heaps of flour, along with twice-born brahmins wearing deerskins.
Adorned with all ornaments, he should, as before, invoke the Viśvādhāma weapon in front of the deity on the right, surrounded by the attendants of Śarva.
From the center up to the northeast, having worshipped with perfumes and flowers,
one should worship the Lord of the Two Hands (Hastadvikeśvara) and Brahmā with the *Ṛg* verses dedicated to Arundhatī.
With joyful hearts, they offered auspicious gifts such as cow udders, chariots, and other articles, accompanied by hymns of praise mingled with the sounds of musical instruments.
With his hand, he [placed] flowers correctly from the soles of the feet up to the crown of the head,
both very high and even higher, as well as very low and even lower.
The Guru, endowed with devotion, should visit Somāskandeśvara along with Viśākha and the God of gods,
or the Lord alone.
Having offered water for sipping and the arghya offering, and having taken [the vessel] consecrated by mantra,
one should rub it with the thumb and ring finger upon the pedestal.
Having performed this three times, one should cast it into the lamp for the pacification of his obstacles;
one should likewise cast it upon the head, the forehead, the throat, the heart, and the two feet.

The wise one should perform the ritual on the navel, both feet, the back, and the region of the hump of the Goddess in sequence; likewise, O Lord, he should perform it on the forehead, the throat, and the shoulder of the Deity.
Then one should give the remaining ashes to Caṇḍā and Prasādhinī; having caused the women and others to carry away the lamps and the extinguishers, [the rite is concluded].
Or they may cast [the remains] before a great sacred seat (mahāpīṭha), or at the edge of a lake, or at the foot of a tree,
accompanied by the sounds of conchs and trumpets and many lamps throughout the day.
The glorious one, possessing the five great sounds and accompanied by mirrors, parasols, and chowries,
being fond of songs, shall be delighted by those hymns and garlands.
One should offer abundant sacrificial oblations accompanied by all ritual services;
one should cause various offerings to be presented individually with abundant materials and the like.
In vessels made of gold, silver, and so forth, beginning from the feet, one should place leaves; likewise, curd, rice, milk-rice, and other foods, ending with vegetables and side-dishes.
At the conclusion, he should offer water for sipping (ācamana) preceded by the wiping of the hands;
then the Guru should offer betel leaf as a mouth-freshener and perform the recitation (japa).
Having offered worship to the deity, one should desire the fruit sought;
having understood that in other tantras the result follows immediately, one should practice after performing worship.
Thus, when performed for a specific purpose, this merit destroys all famine and even eliminates fevers, planetary afflictions, great epidemics, and the like.

Anointing and so forth are to be performed while remaining free from verbal expression; with these substances, one should perform the lustration, as well as the application of unguents, the offering of incense, and the presentation of flowers.
One should offer incense, lamps, fragrant substances,
oblations, and joyful music; furthermore, there are songs, instrumental music, dance, forehead marks, and flowers, making five at the conclusion of the *mātṛkā* recitation.
(29) What is the fivefold purification?
The chariot, the mirror, the parasol, the gift, the recitation, and the divine nectar— these are it.

O Supreme Lord, in the ritual of worshiping Śiva, these thirty-two [deities] have been enjoined as the objects of prostration and the worship of the feet; yet, O Great One, where is that five-faced one [Śiva] who is the witness of all this? Or rather, he is present here.
Thus ends the chapter on the complete propitiation in the *Vijayottara*, within the compendium of sūtras consisting of three thousand verses.
I shall now briefly explain the offering of the auspicious sprout (*maṅgalāṅkura*). That sprout is the root, and its great trunk is the *puṃs* [mantra] ending with *ākāma*.
This [rite] is performed at the installation, during the installation ceremony, at a sacred ford (tīrtha), at the establishment of a shrine, during a great festival,
at the Damanaka festival, at a sacrifice, and also according to the rules for the four-month period (cāturmāsya).
One should plant the sprout of auspiciousness even in another virtuous act;
that is declared to be twofold, according to the division into the manifest and the unmanifest.
Those seeds which were previously [planted] on such-and-such a day, when the fires have not yet been kindled and while the nights are still dark, must be sown by the masters with great care.
He then performed the ritual filling of the seed-vessel (bījapura) at the appropriate time,
including fruits, sprouts, and a coconut flower.

It should be placed in vessels such as *pālikās*, filled with unbroken grains, broken pieces of sugar, sacred threads, or colored powders; or else, it may be arranged like a sprout-plot (*aṅkurārpaṇa*) together with its supporting base.
It is said that the manifest and the unmanifest are distinct, consisting of the sprouts of the elements;
the offering of the divine sprouts is prescribed for the night prior to the day [of the ritual].
It has been stated that at night, under the constellation Ṛkṣa, one should worship Time as the soul of the day, which is the auspicious sprout for mortals,
by means of a jar containing the remains of the deceased and so forth.
The vessel is known as a *ghaṭi* or a *śarāva*; its support is considered to be of three kinds:
made of gold, silver, or copper, or it may consist of any one of these three.
One should fashion eight or four [images] for each [deity], according to one's own capacity. I shall briefly describe that which establishes them, preceded by the measurements.
Beginning from one finger-breadth (aṅgula) for each part,
increasing by one finger-breadth up to twenty [parts], the width and height of that sacred field (kṣetra) are thus proclaimed.
Having divided the field into eighty-one squares with equal courtyards,
the lips, teeth, and the height of the head and so forth are equal to that.
The width of the field is [determined] by the parts of zero, fire, wind, and six, up to the end of earth;
in nine, seven, and five squares, the lines of the borders proceed like a lotus.
The staff (daṇḍa) is one-third [of the height] and pure; its base consists of seven units. The shaping of the bowl (pālikā) is prescribed, and it is said to have the form of a shallow dish (śarāva).

In that regard, thick lips are said to belong to those born under the Pitṛs; they possess ears that are well-formed and contracted, a height reduced by one-fourth [of the circumference], and the *pālī* is considered to be radiant.
The mouth has the form of a water-pot, and the staff and feet follow in due order;
these are marked by the states of Śiva, Vyoman, Ratha, Agni, Indu, Bhāva, Ucca, and Bhavarāga.
I know that the measures for the fruit-bearing lords have been well forgotten;
one should therefore proceed with the measurement of the walls, which are described as being shaped like a water-pot (kalaśa).
One should fashion its face, feet, and navel so that they are exceedingly beautiful;
the mouth and the fire [altar] should be placed in the four directions at a distance of eight finger-breadths.
Having thus described the *ghaṭikā*, I shall now explain the procedure for the *sūpaṇa*.
Having made fifty squares starting from the first square,
one should smear the central cell with cow-dung and the outer squares up to the edge of the lines.
Having placed eight square plots in the outer corners of the eastern and western dwellings,
one should establish there the eight vessels for the *śarāvas* and within them the eight *pālikās*.
Having established the sun, fire, and moon [in their respective positions], and having placed the eight feet in order within the two elephants, one should set the eight ghaṭikās.
The establishment of the Bhadra [mandala] has been declared; now the procedure for the Kṣudra [mandala] is being stated.
Having divided that field into its constituent principles (tattvas), one should mark four squares in the center.
Having established [the center], one should smear the outer line surrounding that;
then, two squares are situated in each of the directions and corners.
One should place the *śarāva*, the *pālikā*, and the *kumbha* in order starting from the northeast (*īśāna*).
In some places, the five *pālikās* have been described by the auspicious Mānavas.
In this manner, one should determine four squares in each direction using the field itself as the unit,
having first decided according to the requirements of the son's time, proceeding in order from here.
Having adorned the trident-weapon and the fierce spade, both collectively and individually,
with garments and other ornaments, one should mount them upon chariots or similar vehicles as appropriate.
With those who were Śaivas, wearing white garments, turbans, and carrying ritual implements, he performed ablutions.
Having held up streams like sprouts before the bull-bannered god,
he was surrounded by Rudra’s daughters and filled with the attendants of Rudra.
It was endowed with the sound of the Veda, filled with the cries of lions,
and proclaimed by those learned in the Vedas through song, dance, and instrumental music.
Adorned with parasols and chowries, provided with incense and lamps, and endowed with various offerings, it was like the [palace] of a king for the sake of the Lord.
Having circumambulated the site, whether it be a palace, a city, or the like,
one should lead [the deity] to a pure riverbank, a lake, or even a garden.
Alternatively, standing at the place for circumambulation facing the northeast,
one should sprinkle the ground there with scented water mixed with sandalwood paste.
Then, having divided [the site] into nine sections, one should worship the earth— consecrated with mantras— in the central square, which serves as the common foundation, or in the first square.
Having worshipped the Astra-mūrti and the hoe with the Hetimantra,
one should dig up the earth and collect it in vessels such as those used for *svālikā*.
Having worshipped them with two, six, or twelve [offerings] while reciting the *hṛdaya-mantra*,
he should afterwards cause them to enter the temple, having been conveyed by elephants or other [vehicles].

Thereafter, one should circumambulate the site clockwise; having examined the internal structure as previously directed from the heart, one should then circumambulate the architect (dhātṛ) or the image (mūrtikā).
(33) If my dwelling is ahead, with the moon as its crest-ornament, then there is no other place for me to go, such as a pavilion or the like that has been constructed.
Then, in the pavilion, one should begin the sowing of seeds even without the daily rite,
according to the desired sequence among the vessels, jars, and so forth.
Thereafter, one should prepare a seat with lotuses, śāli rice, parched grain, sesame seeds, darbha grass, fruits, and sprouts, arranged in a square formation.
Having adorned the seat in the center, one should worship the seat of the Praṇava;
having placed it in the midst of all the souls, it is as enchanting as a moonlit lake.
One should wrap it with thread up to the ankles using fragrant waters;
it should be adorned with garlands and cloth, and contain a golden disc marked with the moon.
The supreme vessel, consisting of the form of the Moon, should be provided with a lid and a wick-holder,
adorned with five sprouts of dūrvā grass and garlands of caṇḍā flowers.
Durvā grass, flowers, and unbroken grains (akṣata), as well as kuśa grass worshipped by Caṇḍa;
filled with the eight forms (of Śiva), they bring the full moon and destroy the twins.
One should arrange sixty-four shallow bowls in successive order;
then, having sprinkled them with drops of water for the fragrant offering (arghya), one should perform the rite for an auspicious day (puṇyāha).
In the belly of the child at the time of death, there is a continuous stream of cold fire;
gentle and resembling a kunda flower, it is the source of the jar's production.

One should perform the ritual worship of the pervasion and the action, consisting of seven leftward repetitions of the syllable "Śabda" ending with the principle of *mātrā*, while forming the mental resolve directed inwardly during the Rohiṇī constellation.
Having offered incense, flowers, and so forth, as well as milk-rice oblation (pāyasa-havis), betel leaf, and mouth-perfume to Sthāṇu at the end, one should again consecrate Soma with mantras.
Oṃ! With the moonlight of the moon, you have caused the three worlds to arise from the net [of emanation].
For the sake of bestowing the fruit of other seeds, make the beginning of the face complete.
In the Cāturvargamarda, Maheśa has stated:

"Having worshipped those who possess power, one should first take— according to one's ability— one portion each of parched grain, lentils, mung beans, black gram, rice, cooked rice, sesame seeds, and so forth."
Having placed milk in a vessel, one obtains mental peace, water, and power.
Having sprinkled [the object] with the Astra-mantra and anointed it with the Hṛdaya-mantra,
and having worshipped it with the Soma-bīja, one should display the Dhenu-mudrā.
Thereafter, the preceptor should offer the seeds with their respective mantras,
having invoked the Lord Śiva by those who follow the path of the Śaiva Siddhānta.
Or one may cause the Veda to be recited by those established in Brahman who have mastered the Vedas,
accompanied by conchs, kambala-drums, and other musical instruments, along with those chanting hymns of praise and auspicious verses.
Having offered betel-leaf and flowers accompanied by auspicious sprouts,
and having meditated upon the filled pitcher, he should thereafter offer kusha grass and other items.
Having thoroughly sprinkled the auspicious lake Candrakumbha with water from jars, he remained there, as it were, sowing the seeds of happiness with drops of earth.
Having worshipped the deity again, and having restrained him for the sake of the wound,
one should satisfy him by offering food prescribed for the dwelling of the Kuṇṭaka, along with seals and other such items.
In whatever region this is performed, rain falls in that place at the proper time; pestilences do not prevail there— how much more so, my dear, when the *aṅga* [mantra] is deposited?
Perhaps the pain of separation might not occur for a husband and wife on this earth;
however, what is the use of saying more? Wealth is the sprout from the seed of illusion (māyā).
The desires of all living beings always increase in accordance with that sequence.
Thus ends the chapter on the offering of sprouts (*aṅkurārpaṇa*) in the *Vijayottara*, the compendium of three thousand verses.
The Chapter on the Ritual for the Festival of Śiva:
Now I shall explain in detail the sequence of the ritual for the festival of Śiva,
which liberates living beings from the bondage of attachment to the impurity of ignorance.
The production of knowledge for them is considered a festival,
because it brings about an arisen creation and because it wards off suffering.
It is proclaimed to be threefold: obligatory (nitya), occasional (naimittika), and optional (kāmya).
That which is performed at the conclusion of the obligatory worship is called the obligatory (nitya) rite.
In the months beginning with Caitra, the ritual procedure is performed on the first day of each respective month;
for kings, the occasional rite (naimittika) should be performed at the beginning and end of the lunar mansions (nakṣatra) that mark their birth and death.
The wise one understands that the rule for optional (kāmya) rites is performed for the sake of accomplishing a desired object;
this is the distinction between the occasional (naimittika) and the optional (kāmya) rites by their very nature.

Therefore, whatever statement regarding occasional rites (naimittika) or optional rites (kāmya) may be made, it should be understood as lacking an injunction; and among these three types of rites, the obligatory (nitya) is declared to be the foremost.

The occasional festival (naimittikotsava) of the Supreme Lord will be described at the beginning and the end [of the year]. [It occurs] on the days of Citrā, Viśākhā, Mūla, and Uttarāṣāḍhā, until the end of the day. (p. 36)
Likewise, from Śravaṇa through Puṣya, Āśvinī, and ending with Kṛttikā.
O Lord, a wise person should perform the festival in the months beginning with Meṣa (Aries) in successive order, starting from Puṣya and Maghā and ending with Uttarā.
In all months except Jyeṣṭha, [the ceremony] should end with Ārdrā; in Jyeṣṭha, it should end with Śatabhiṣaj.
The consecration of a king and his departure [from the city] should take place at the conclusion of the three birth-stars.
O god of the world, even if it be a constellation ending in the letter *n*, a wise man should choose it as the time for a great emperor, provided his mind is inclined toward it.

The solar month (saura-māsa) is recommended for the period ending on that day and for the conclusion of the installation of that liṅga; however, the lunar month (cāndra-māsa) is recommended for one who desires excellence.
When two lunar mansions coincide within a single month, it is most excellent;
for in such a case, the power of the conjunction is complete, provided that the conjunction is likewise favorable.
In the former [rite] as well, it should be performed according to one's wealth;
there, Mahādeva should be bathed, especially on the sacred festival days (parvan).

Having observed [the auspicious time], one should designate the sacred site (*tīrtha*); the two [types] have been briefly described to you. Likewise, the hoisting of the banner (*dhvajāroha*) and the *tīrtha* ceremony may take place in either one month or two months.
The last day of that period is most auspicious; if it occurs earlier, it brings destruction to the performer. [This applies] on the first, third, fifth, seventh, ninth, or tenth days.
Likewise, among the fifteen days, the names are given in their respective order elsewhere as the Śaiva, the Gauṇa, the Vibhūti, the Bhauvana, and the Daivika.
Then, dividing it again into three types— namely, the paternal (*paitṛka*), the victorious (*vijaya*),
and the *puṣkala* called *vijaya*, as well as the *kevala*— in due order:

One should designate the night prior to the day specified for the consecration as the time for the preliminary ritual (adhivāsana); and where there is a festival for the image, one should specify that it lasts until the very end.

That very [ceremony] they call Bhramaṇi; according to its influence during festivals such as Pakṣotsava, it is further divided into three types based on distinctions such as the hoisting of the flag and so forth.
One should avoid the *śaiva*, *bhauṇa*, and *vibhūti* nakṣatras for the hoisting of the banner;
rather, one should begin the hoisting of the banner during the *bhauvana* and *dvijaya* nakṣatras.
In that regard, for each day and its double,
the wise one should perform the festival in successive order, preceded by the offering of the ritual sprouts (aṅkurārpaṇa).
Having hoisted the banner on that day and beaten the drum at night,
the commencement of the festival takes place at night, beginning with the ritual sowing of sprouts for the theater.
The wise man should understand that first there is the raising of the banner;
previously the treasure was described, and after the drum, the ritual for the banner.
Having performed the offering of sprouts there as before during the night,
the striking of the drum should precede the offering of sprouts at night.
On an auspicious day prior to the day of raising the flag, and before the descent [of the deity],
one should collect the timber according to the procedure prescribed for that ritual.
Having entered a forest or a garden that is suitable and conducive to tranquility during the early part of the night, the preceptor, together with the artisans, [should proceed].
Having worshipped and gratified the tree with the *bhūmyastra* mantra combined with the *caṇḍanātha* mantra, one should bind the protective thread (*kautuka*) while reciting the *hṛdaya* mantra.
Then, at the clear dawn, Muru, equipped with his trident weapon,
performed worship as before and dismissed the forest deity.
Having cut with that well-sharpened axe while reciting the Mṛtyujit mantra,
one should subsequently have it carved by artisans who are experts in the science of architecture (vāstu-vidyā).
One should examine his foot according to the distinction between the auspicious and inauspicious directions;
it is not auspicious when the inner leaf, water, or wind [of the foot] points toward the intermediate directions.
In the morning, having offered the remainder of the tree [offerings] to the directions for the sake of the beauty of the quarters,
one should first worship the preceptor with garments, gold, and rings.
Thereafter, one should honor the astrologer and have people offer betel leaves;
thus, having planted trees and other plants during the auspicious months, [one should transport them] by means of carts and similar vehicles.
Then, having established the workshop, one should construct the Vindatī, Karatha,
and other structures during those days and auspicious moments, accompanied by auspicious rites.
In that regard, the vehicle consists of water-pots and the like; the momentary support is the dwelling;
and likewise the enclosure wall, the gate-tower, the hall, the pavilion, and so forth, which constitute the interior space.
The attendants, the couch, the throne, and that bull—these are difficult to accomplish;
they are bound together by a foundation made of a mass of lime mixed with resin.
Therefore, having made it white, one should decorate it with various colors where the Lord establishes his assembly hall for the sake of his adorned pastimes.
In various places, pavilions and other structures should be constructed with great beauty;
they should be adorned with colored lines drawn upon a base smeared with ghee and *sāghrakeśa*.
It was provided with a canopy, a parasol, and adorned with garlands.
Surrounded on all sides by auspicious Vaijayantī banners as she ascended,
she was adorned with gold and jewels and arrayed in variegated silken garments.
O God, the chariot-wheels of the Lord of Gods must be made of flowers;
various kinds of mechanical devices should be constructed separately.
Then, having consecrated the sun with an oblation, the wise man should perform the recitation (japa) over one made of wood or hide; he may also make it of stone, clay, or brick.
Having first offered the sprouts according to the previously mentioned procedure, the preceptor,
the teacher, should then perform the sacrifice of the bull after informing Śiva.

On the day before the hoisting of the banner, having worshipped the bull with perfumes and other offerings brought [for that purpose] while it stands before Śiva, one should tie the protective amulet (kautuka) upon it— or alternatively, [upon the officiant].
Having bound [the image] with the Śṛṅgeśavṛṣa mantra, either at the front or at the back,
in a place free from disturbances, [one should fill it] with śāli rice, taṇḍula rice, and sesame seeds.
There, having made a resolve according to the requirements of the location, one should separately establish two sacrificial altars (*sthaṇḍila*);
their characteristics are stated here.
Visible, white, subtle, and fashioned by makers, the world’s ancient banner has perished; one should bring it back as it was before.
From the Śivadhvaja, one should extend the dimensions for the [deities] ending with Lipta by a tenth part and so forth,
joined with their respective vehicles according to their individual colors.
Red, yellow, or black, having been heard by the Vasus through their great austerities,
he is perfectly endowed with the flavors that produce all beings and is covered with hair like feathers.

Furthermore, the banner for all the gods, beginning with the deities, should be made according to the measurement of an ikṣu (sugarcane) during festivals, the installation of images, and other such occasions.
All items such as banners and cloths shall be made by the authority of the Superintendent of the Granary,
using auspicious threads woven by maidens born of his own lineage.
The ritual beginning with the *pavitrārohaṇa* is established everywhere;
in the measurement, it is forgotten by one part out of five, six, or seven parts.
It may be equal in measurement to that, or perhaps slightly less or greater;
it may be provided with a pinnacle half its size, or even have its summit consisting of a portion of that.
Equipped with two bamboo poles at its top like a rope-pulley mechanism,
having thus raised the banner, one should draw a bull in its center.
Having divided the two doors into nine parts according to their respective proportions,
one should fashion the nine measures beginning with the *jyeṣṭha* and ending with the *kanyasā*.
Having extended the wall up to the edge of the mouth-opening by eight finger-breadths,
the wise one should fashion the divisions for the kalā, kola, and bhāga, and so forth.
Whether standing or reclining according to the method prescribed in the treatises on arts,
he should be seated in the lotus posture (padmāsana), with lamps and other offerings arranged at his side.

The wise one [should fashion the image] as endowed with a parasol and chowries, accompanied by full water-jars and the self-luminous [deity], and either provided with trident-weapon emblems or devoid of them.
Having had it fashioned by an artisan, one should perform the opening of the eyes in this manner;
having sprinkled it with water of the Puṣya asterism and established it with the water of Śiva.
Having sprinkled [the bull] with the Vṛṣamantra, the Guru should worship it with scents and other offerings;
then, having prepared a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) in front of it, he should place nine jars that have been filled with water.
The two Lords of the World (Lokeshvaras) are lost on the bull; one should worship them all around the center.
In front of that, on a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila), the Guru should perform the fire-oblation (homa) with fuel-sticks of *arudhra* wood.
Having offered oblations one hundred times— or even fifty or twenty-five— using the *vṛṣa-gāyatrī* mantra, he should place a staff before her and perform the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsana*).
The height up to the pinnacle may be twice, three times, or equal to the base;
or it may extend to the end of the nose, the end of the neck, or be equal to the bull-platform.
In houses with many stories, the height may extend from four, three, or two storeys up to nine cubits,
or alternatively, starting from nine cubits, it may go up to fifteen cubits.
It should be made of bamboo, heartwood, or blameless *kramuka* wood;
it should measure twelve finger-breadths and so forth, be radiant, and be endowed with an auspicious name.

One should take a bamboo staff (vaiṇava) or a betel-nut staff (kramuka) according to one's own measurement, with dimensions of twelve, twelve, nine, six, and four finger-breadths (aṅgulas), respectively, for the Lord of the Gods, the Sun, the Moon, Mercury, and Jupiter.
It is joined with three skandas, which are long, spread out, half-moon shaped, and bound by wealth, possessing apertures as appropriate to their form.
According to their strength and according to their beauty,
they were attached to the handles of the ladles and bowls by means of cords and mechanical devices.
It is provided with a blue iron band;
the cause for the bracelet is the thumb, not the cord.
One who is fit for the practice of raising the banner and is endowed with good fortune.

Having joined it with a garland of *darbha* grass and sprinkled it with water while reciting the *astra-mantra*, one should then worship it with perfumes and other offerings, accompanied by auspicious sounds such as the word "Victory! (*jaya*).
Between the pedestal and the gateway, or between the bull and the gateway,
or at the front of the pedestal, or at the front of the bull, or even behind both of them.
Having dug a pit measuring four *tālas* in depth and cleared of all impure soil,
one should place a golden tortoise within it with the *praṇava*.
Having fixed the staff with a mechanical device, construct an altar at its base;
it may be made of stone, or of bricks on the sides, or otherwise provided with bricks on all sides.
[The altar] should be one cubit up to three cubits in length, with a width of three finger-breadths,
increasing by one-eighth [of its length] up to eight parts, and decreasing by five [parts] at the end.
The width, rising higher and higher in ascending degrees, is adorned with thirty-five parts;
from the first part up to the end of Rudra, it is measured by single units.
One should construct [the altar] at the base of the *patopāna* or at *mekhalāvatī*,
either according to the *mānāṅgula* or by means of the *mātrāṅgula*.
Having prepared the sacrificial altar and performed the dismissal of the artisans,
one should smear it with cow dung and decorate it with colored powders.
Having sprinkled it with pure water, one should perform the preliminary consecration (adhivāsana) on the previous night;
or alternatively, one may perform the preliminary consecration for the flagstaff immediately.
Having thus accepted [the offering], one should then give a village adorned with all ornaments and joined with a trident, or else an oblation (*bali*).

At dawn, at the conclusion of the daily worship, having adorned the banner with flowers and other offerings and having worshipped it with perfumes and so forth, one should offer an oblation of mung-bean rice.
