One should present betel leaf, mouth-freshener, the glorious sound of the five great instruments, a parasol, a mirror, and chowries.
Having meditated upon Śakti, who has the form of the support of the phenomenal world, beginning with Kalā and ending with Śiva, as well as the bull and the trident-bearing God of gods in person;
Having placed [the body] upon the shoulder of a palanquin, or in a palanquin, or on chariots,
accompanied by various musical instruments and endowed with various songs.
One should offer the bali-oblation to the lords of the directions, accompanied by the weapons and the forms [of the deities].
Having thus performed the circumambulation, one should enter the interior of the sanctuary.
Having circumambulated the village with the banner joined to the sacrificial mound and accompanied by the chanting of the Vedas, and having entered the place where the staff is stationed;
When the auspicious moment had been released by the gods, bestowing blessings upon the patron,
he caused the proclamation of a holy day (*puṇyāha*) and sprinkled [the site] with that water.
Having meditated upon the staff as consisting of the body of knowledge (vidyādeha), one should worship it with perfumes and other offerings;
and in the four directions of that staff, accompanied by the sounds of dancing and singing—
Having fastened it with a rope-mechanism and equipped it with a banner and bell,
one should take up the Vṛṣa-mantra and place the water-pot upon the heart of the bull.
Having worshipped with perfumes and other offerings, and then with the chanting of the Brahmins' Vedic recitations,
the practitioner of mantras should hoist the banner, neither too quickly nor too slowly.
One should join the water from the jars of the world-protectors (lokapāla) starting from the base of the staff;
having worshipped the weapon (astra) with perfumes and other offerings, and having offered green gram rice (mudgānna).
One should afterwards address the Banner (Dhvaja) for wandering here and there;
even by one who is unstable, this twofold task must be performed for the sake of attaining enjoyment and liberation.
At this time, the wise one should also cause the banner of the temple to be raised;
at the moment of hoisting the banner, an offering is made to the bull.
And having eaten of it, one shall obtain a son who is a portion of Īśvara; there is no doubt regarding this, wherever this installation of the flagstaff is performed in a kingdom.
Therein, there is no untimely death, nor misfortune even among evildoers;
the rain falls in its proper season, there is abundance of food, and the king is victorious.
Having placed the Lord together with Bhavānī upon a palanquin or similar vehicle,
accompanied by banners and all auspicious articles, [one should proceed].
Having circumambulated the city, one should enter the assembly pavilion;
having performed the sequence of service with the appropriate ritual offerings as is fitting.
Furthermore, when the sun has set, having completed the ritual portion pertaining to the evening,
one should begin the sounding of the kettledrums once the hour (muhūrta) has duly arrived.

Either in front of the deity or in front of the liṅga, having prepared two altars (sthaṇḍila) with śāli rice, unhusked rice, and sesame seeds, and adorned them with flowers for the womb and other ornaments;
Having exhausted the weapon-mantra upon a single [target], the Guru should worship it with perfumes and other offerings;
he should then place before it a drum that is faultless and possesses the characteristics described in the scriptures.
One should conceive of two faces on the left side, one at the front and one at the back;
then, according to the body's orientation, one should likewise assign the solar and lunar faces.
Having caused the declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) to be recited and having sprinkled [the site] with water,
one should place the seed-syllable of Nandin in the center, and those of Saura and Candra at the two mouths.

Having worshipped Nandikeśa with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings up to the food oblation (naivedya), the practitioner of mantra, endowed with devotion, should worship him according to the excellent mantra.
O you whose sound is like the roar of a drum, O giver of supreme bliss, O Nandika!
O Nandīśvara, salutations to you, the three-eyed, great-souled one.
First, the Guru, having invoked him with the *santāsa-hetu* mantra three times,
should summon one who is pure and endowed with the *śaiva-dīkṣā*.
Having sprinkled [the area] with scented water, one should properly cast [the obstacles] away with the thighs;
then, with the five sounds of drums and other instruments, accompanied by the skillful conduct of those seeking happiness.
Having cast that flower there and having mentally disregarded that which is censured,
one who is skilled in the science of musical instruments should play while maintaining a pleasant countenance.
The dancer, the presser, the singer, the flute-player,
and Taṇḍimoravika— these are declared to be the five teachers.
In the ritual of the five preceptors, the castes are arranged in their natural order on all sides,
accompanied by various musical instruments, stringed instruments, and the beating of kettledrums and tabors.
There was a tumultuous roar from jhallarī cymbals and other instruments,
as well as from lutes, flutes, mṛdaṅga drums, conchs, kāhala trumpets, and kacakka drums.
O Indra,
O Lord, may we be purified by the many utterances of the glorious *Pañcamahāyajña*, which grant the fulfillment of the Vedas and the sacred hymns.
Let one person play the instruments of the *śānta*, *sama*, and *tāla* rhythms,
as well as the drum covered with leather, the *sakta*, the *dharaṇa*, and the flute.
The wise know these five as the Great Sounds (Mahāśabda);
in some places, they have been proclaimed by the Supreme Lord (Parameṣṭhin) under those very names.
Then, for the satisfaction of the respective guardians of the quarters,
he sang the *uditālagīta* and the *mallatālaka* of Bhṛṅgin, which were merged within Brahman.
Navākhyo, Bali, Tāla, Choṭitāla,
Caḍhakkarī, Gaurī, Kuṭivarādī, Kūrjarī, and likewise Bheripa.
Deśāri, Śīrṣa, and Trayanta—these are said to be the [first] three *gānas*. Then there are Antāli, Megha, Nāga, Kolli, Kauśika, and Pañcama.
Śālaka, Naṭṭanāga, and Tuṅganāga are known as the Tālakeyas,
extending from Brahmā to Īśāna.
Then, having first summoned the gods with a mantra,
the preceptor or his disciple should prepare the sacrificial offering (bali) and the necessary materials.
One should perform a circumambulation of the village while accompanied by the form of the Astra-mantra;
one should offer oblations (bali) to the lords of the directions with pure boiled rice mixed with clarified butter.
O wise ones, let all the guardians of the directions and the constellations be informed;
with the sounding of kettledrums, let the day be given for the movement of the army.
Therefore, living beings who possess discernment should not go there under any circumstances;
from that [place] comes the auspiciousness of the Lord of Gods, which draws forth the sacred ford on the left.
Therefore, others who desire health should perform bathing at sacred fords (tīrthas);
however, this rule does not apply to a universal monarch (cakravartin) or a great king.
Even for men, when [the Self] is supreme through effort within the self,
and when that Lord of Gods has not been struck down by the self, there shall be no internal banner in the state of Bhava, nor in the mounting of the banner.
At the auspicious hour for the deities, there shall likewise be an auspicious time for the king;
this occurs after the completion of the sacrifice and the removal of obstacles, following the day of the flag-hoisting.
Furthermore, a wise person should certainly not observe fasts, festivals,
and the like during that time when a great sacrifice has already been commenced.
The sacrificial pit, weapons, and fire should be prepared; there is no separate night for sacrifice.
One should perform the worship of the Lord of Sacrifice and the fire-oblation (homa) with double the usual measure.
Then one should perform the rite for the emergence of the image; no other speech is desired.
For the sake of the sacrifice, one should construct a pavilion with a canopy and banners as it is prescribed.
Then I shall describe everything here; Śarva is Indra, O best of speakers, for he is proclaimed elsewhere as well to be the creator in the form of the reclining one.
The youngest, the middle, and the eldest—each of these three types may further be divided into three;
thus, from five to twenty-one cubits, there are nine distinct efforts.
Pride is external, internal, or intermediate; having entered further, it becomes manifold.
Regarding devotion therein, it is like pillars, pure cloths, or pavements.
Ghanoghoṣadhī, Rāga, Kāñcana, Kāmarāmaka, Sughoṣā, Sarvarodakṣā, and Maṇṭapa— these are the nine Mānatās.
The sacrificial hall may be made of stone, brick, or clay;
it should be well-proportioned, provided with an exit, inner chambers, a courtyard, and archways.
One should understand that there is a water-tank with openings on the four sides, adorned with a porch, and its doors are oriented toward the east, north, and west within the cardinal directions.
The courtyard floor was entirely covered by spreading shade;
it was a magnificent sacrificial hall, complete with well-proportioned architectural members.
O Lord, one should have it fashioned by skilled artisans using various types of diverse molds, provided with nine crucibles.
Whether it be fashioned by the five [deities] or not subject to the distinction of forms,
one should adorn the sacrificial pavilion all around with their respective mandalas.
One should place [the syllables] beginning with Śānti, Bhūti, Bala, Ārogya, and Saṃjñānita;
it consists of three parts, ending with five, by increasing [the number of syllables] foot by foot.
The arches, vast for the sake of height, cover over those that are deficient as if they were excessive;
they are fashioned from various species of trees, such as the *paya* and *vṛkṣa*, according to their distinct types.
The extensive expansion of the branches should range from two finger-breadths up to twelve finger-breadths;
beyond eight finger-breadths, the hands, the heavy spear-heads, and the prongs are placed above.
On the upper branches, one should place Vināyaka in the center of the forehead,
Śrī on its right side, and Vāgīśvarī on the left side.
On the two sides, one should place a svastika, a lotus, or a blue lotus;
however, in the absence of trees, one may use whatever is available according to the prescribed measure.

Whether for one's own sake or for the sake of others, one should construct archways (toraṇas) endowed with the eight auspicious symbols (aṣṭamaṅgala), equipped with the vajra weapon, and provided with a chariot.
With streams flowing from vessels filled with water, resting upon three-legged stands,
spread with the sprouts of the [six] commands and adorned with fruits;
At each door, one should decorate the full water-jars with plantain pillars that resemble the rainbow of Indra,
the bandūka flower, and dark blue clouds.
Adorned with banners of Śiva resembling golden lotuses,
one should perform the rite after sprinkling [the area] with water and facing the sun.
One should meditate upon the pavilion as the abode of Śaṅkara, consisting of the kalās such as Nirvṛti, as Sadāśiva himself, manifest, adorned with the banner and marked by Śakti.
In the middle of that, one should construct a single temple according to one's devotion,
measuring three, four, or five cubits, with its width being one-third of that [length].
They should be one cubit in height, or raised by the span of a fist,
and provided with a small ledge according to their beauty and proportions.
One should construct fire-pits around [the central area], smooth and pure like the surface of a mirror, according to the divisions of nine, five, or one.
On the five [altars], one should arrange the placement of the sacrificial altars (*vedi*), the crescent moon, the triangle, and the circle;
these should be well-proportioned, with their corners facing the directions, starting from the southeast.
The ninth [mandala] in the center should be circular, as should those between the two bull-emblems (Śivas);
everywhere else, they should be square and circular.
If one [desires] a square, a circle, or a lotus, [the measurements] are respectively four, three,
and two finger-breadths on the outside.
There are three intermediate spokes, each six finger-breadths long, or perhaps only one;
upon them, facing north, are the navel, the nave, and the axle-hole.
On these, facing east, other [seats] were spread out on all sides according to their beauty,
distinguished by the altar, the archways, and the sacrificial pits.
The preceptor should determine the measurement using either the *mānāṅgula* or the *mātrāṅgula*;
once it has been thus constructed, he should perform the dismissal of the artisan.
In a sacrificial pavilion that has been smeared with cow dung, provided with the performance of the *homa* rite,
consecrated by the *puṇyāha* ceremony, and rendered pure;

The festival culminating in victory for those beginning with the Śaivas and ending with the Vijayas is of the nature of victory; it is performed according to the desire of the performer, starting from the hoisting of the banner.
On the twelfth day, having performed the propitiation to remove obstacles according to the prescribed rite,
the preceptor should offer various types of knowledge-removing oblations and make his request.
O Blessed One, I am the great festival of this Mādi Śaiva; I have set in motion [this rite] until the end of the elements, and all obstacles are present in your presence.
Having thus prayed to Vighneśa, who is endowed with all auspiciousness,
and having circumambulated the village, the Blessed One then entered it.
One should tie the *kautuka* (sacred thread) upon Soma, or upon one who bears the crescent moon;
or indeed, it may be tied upon an *utpāta-dhauka*, or even upon another, according to the desire of the performer.
In a land crowded with thieves and the like, or in a desert, one should bathe the Lord of the gods, who is adorned with white garments, using either only a trident-weapon or [other means].
Having prepared the sacrificial offering (bali) with white upper garments and even garlands at the base of the pavilion,
he should then place [the deity] before it upon a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) made of rice.
One should worship vessels made of gold, silver, and so forth, having filled them with rice;
having placed them upon a tripod, one should set the marriage-thread (kautuka) above them.
It may be made of gold or silver, or produced from linen or cotton threads;
it should weigh one niṣka, half of that, or half of that again, or consist of five or three strands.
First, having applied ashes and betel leaf, one should cause the twice-born to recite the *puṇyāha* (auspicious day) formula;
then, having worshipped with perfumes and other offerings using the *Hṛdaya-mantra*, the region becomes the embodiment of the mantra.
Wearing a turban and an upper garment, adorned with earrings and other ornaments, one should offer abundant betel-leaf; for what else could be more serviceable to men?
When the auspicious moment had arrived, Tryambaka,
having consecrated that ash with mantras and meditated upon it as the bridegroom’s wedding bracelet, applied it [to his own body].
A friend should tie the *koṭuka* (amulet) on the right hand of the deity,
while meditating on the form of the Goddess’s crescent moon upon her left lotus-hand.
p.
52) If Skanda, Nandīśa, and Caṇḍeśa are situated at his sides,
one should also join them with their respective mantras in the right hand.
O Lord, one may offer even a small portion of ashes that destroy the Rākṣasas according to worldly custom;
yet here, that ash is not distinct [from the sacred ash], for through devotion it leads to the path of devotion on the fourteenth day of the lunar fortnight.
They delight all the ancestors and gladden the three Yamalas,
endowed with all auspiciousness and the weapons of the lords of the astral world.
In this manner, one should bathe the Lord of Gods with the three sweet juices,
with sacred waters, and also with perfumed water mixed with camphor.
Having sprinkled water all around the temple of the Āgama with the Astra-mantra,
and having performed worship upon the door-frames, he should install the guardians of the gates.
Having entered within, one should prepare an excellent sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) in the northeast;
above that, one should place the weapon-mantra (astra), surrounded by the weapons of the world-protectors (lokeśa).
Having worshipped with offerings beginning with perfumes and flowers and ending with oblations,
one should prepare the Śiva-fire in the northeast, or in the center between Īśāna and Śaṃbhu.
Having meditated upon [the deity] as consisting of all forms, one should satisfy [him] with sacrificial fuel sticks and other offerings;
[specifically] with palāśa fuel sticks ending with clarified butter, and then with parched grain and sesame seeds.
Having offered the food of King Siddhārthamaka to Śiva in the proper sequence of the limbs,
and having at the end of that offered betel-leaf and performed the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti), [one should proceed].
Then, at the conclusion of the internal offering, having caused the youth Agni to be restrained and having instructed him regarding the materials for the offering,
one should again present the village offering.
p.
53) Wherever there are twelve [deities] beginning with Brahmā and ending with Īśāna,
whether in a village endowed with many kinds of rites, in its center, or outside of it;
One should perform the offering (bali) according to the ritual sequence and as appropriate through investigation,
distributing it around the crossroads and along the rows of stakes.

The knower of mantras, according to the prescribed rule, should perform [the rite] with pure *daṇḍakas* from the east to the northeast, using the aforementioned substances for the lords of those respective days.

Having mounted upon this chariot, which is adorned with peacock feathers and other ornaments, the weapon of the material elements (dravyāstra) and the weapon of the world-protectors (lokapālāstra), together with the sacrificial food (anna) and the ritual emblem (liṅga).
Accompanied by the loud resounding of sacrificial drums that strike fear into the enemies of the gods,
one should circumambulate the village clockwise and sequentially cast the offering for the spirits (bhūtabali).
Then the preceptor, having been honored with food mixed with clarified butter or curd-rice by Śuddhodana,
should offer the village oblation (grāmabali) and enter [the village] at its conclusion.
One should offer the bali-oblation at the great seat (mahāpīṭha), and having entered elsewhere than that,
[one should worship] the yakṣas and others with their respective mantras.
Having cast away the weapon-mantra (astra) along with its gender-indicators, one should deposit all [the offerings] according to the prescribed rules.
Having thus offered the bali-oblation, whether in the morning or even at evening—
At the conclusion of that, one should have a great festival performed for the deity in villages and other places,
featuring various kinds of great jewels, Vedic hymns, gold, garments, and so forth.
It was abundantly covered with many fine garments of dukūla, paṭṭa, and cotton,
and adorned with divine ornaments made of jewels, such as crowns and other regalia.
Adorned with various garlands whose fragrance was not yet fully manifest,
he dispelled all the asuras by the light of his eye on the forehead.
By the gift of his right foot, he [Śiva] became Hara, whose left side was occupied by Gaurī— the bee clinging to the lotus-face of Umā— and who fulfilled the great desires of the multitude.
He was awakening all living beings who had fallen under the power of the sleep of passion, just as the sun awakens the lotus buds.
Having brought him upon a palanquin and other such vehicles, accompanied by the sounds of Vedic hymns and musical instruments,
and with a bright parasol held above him with a golden handle;
With the mass of light from its bracelets cast aside, yet attended by fly-whisks and various retinues,
it was like a great assembly of kings.
It was adorned by Apsarases walking before him,
fanning golden garments upon his bones.
Thus, with devotion, he chewed the lotuses that had reached their full bloom.
It was adorned and crowded with people who offered hymns of praise,
and it was filled with large-eyed women whose beauty stole away the luster of blue lotuses.
The Lord of the festival was being worshipped by the citizens with blooming smiles—
now by the Śaivas near the attendant, and now by the Bhairava-Tantrikas.
[It was attended] by those on the left, who abide on the path of the Kula, who know the meaning of the Bhūta-tantras,
who are teachers and knowers of the path of the Sairis, and in some places, proponents of the inner self (adhyātma).
It is attended by those belonging to the Vedas, by worldly people, and by others concerned with the next world and so forth,
who follow their respective paths of established doctrine and offer praise.
His prowess was being praised by various kinds of Piśācas, as well as by Kāma, Kāla, Anukarṣaṇa, Tripuradhvaṃsana, and others.
[He saw] the foremost leaders of the city who had rescued [others] from the ocean of saṃsāra,
whose ground was purified by the tips of their hair that had been soiled while playing in the sands.
With waters mixed with sandalwood, saugandhika, and utpala lotuses,
as if sprinkled by clouds, she performed the sequence of all auspicious rites.
The entire residence was strewn with banners, garlands, and wreaths of darbha grass;
it was adorned with rows of tinkling bells and uplifted great flags.
It had golden archways supported by pillars made of areca-nut trees and banana trunks,
and was adorned at every door with lamps, incense burners, water-jars, and other offerings.
Having perfumed the directions with incense, fragrance, and so forth,
one should indeed, in due order, offer divine water, betel-leaf, and mouth-fresheners.
At every crossroads, beginning with the morning twilight (saṃdhyā), one should repeatedly offer oblations to the deity at that time, accompanied by the appropriate conduct for each occasion.
One should perform the circumambulation of the site (vāstu), beginning from the north-east, where the head of Soma and the crescent moon are located;
in that place, if one makes it copper-colored, it bestows ancient merit.
And the most wealthy person should have a festival for the image performed right there,
provided that the distant location is not separated by a river or other such obstacles from the sky.
56) Even elsewhere, by means of that same consecration, one brings about a great festival;
for what need is there to construct a dwelling in a place crowded with frost, wandering thieves, and the like?

Having performed the ritual of the bali offering here, one should carry out the pacifying fire-oblation (śāntihoma). At its conclusion, O God of gods, one should cause the assembly pavilion to be constructed.
One should worship the God of gods, the Lord of the universe, seated upon an auspicious throne in a pavilion,
or on a stage, or in a charming water-shed.
Adorned with fine linen garments, flowers, canopies, and other ornaments,
and having prepared the surrounding enclosure according to the prescribed ritual rules, one should proceed there.

Having offered water for the feet, water for sipping, and water for the face to the deity as before, one should, with a concentrated mind, perform worship according to the appropriate ritual services.

During the festival of the artisans' workshop, one should perform ablutions and rites for peace and fire-offerings (homa) morning and evening, according to one's ability, with gold ornaments, garments, and other offerings.
One should pass the time with dance, instrumental music, song, and so forth;
having spent four days in this manner, on the fifth day—
Having brought Maheśvara, adorned with all ornaments, to the bank of a river, or to a grove, or to a charming field;
Facing east, she went to the ground to fetch the desired command;
one should worship the Earth at each respective step, having meditated upon her form as previously described.
Then, one should consecrate the ground with the Pṛthvī-bīja and with perfumes and other offerings:
"Oṃ! O auspicious one, O you of sweet fragrance, O blessed one, O you who abide as the refuge of all that is auspicious!"
"O Goddess, bestower of all desires, remain steadfast for the king.
Having thus worshipped with perfumes and other offerings, one should then address the Goddess.
May the king be victorious; may the earth also flourish;
and may all his subjects be happy, becoming ever more so in succession.

The most excellent Guru should extract the desired earth situated within the pit, which is the very embodiment of its wealth, along with gold, silver, and other treasures in vessels, using the seed-syllable of that [deity].
"Thus, O best of kings, I shall bring you down to the surface of the earth;
this is the supreme distinction of the Victorious One, whose nature is the weapon of sacrifice."
This is the eternal rule for collecting the clay for the sake of the sprouts:
on the third day, one should [prepare] the cloth and the image together with Caṇḍa.
Led by those who were portions of Maheśa, wearing turbans and carrying golden vessels and other supports for the sprouts, which were beautifully adorned and placed before them.
Having circumambulated the site clockwise, and having sprinkled the ground with water from the *nityodgāna* and other vessels, he should dig up the earth with a spade using the *heti* mantra.
Having taken it and led it to his abode,
the most excellent preceptor goes there at sunset, having first performed the ritual offering of the *kuśa* grass according to the prescribed rite.

In an auspicious moment and at a favorable *lagna*, one should begin the extensive ritual of the *āgama*; however, if the full requirements for the ritual have not been obtained, one may proceed with the great festival of the *astra-āgama*.
Who indeed will conquer the enemies with this most terrible Anarcya weapon,
by means of the infallible sacrifice of weapons, since the king’s weapons have been rendered unfailing?
The root banners have a measurement of four, five, or six parts;
or else, they are characterized by the weapons and vehicles of the guardians of the directions.
In the eight directions, there should be betel-leaves, palaces, and so forth, along with eight banners;
within the courtyard, in the center, there should be a pearl necklace on the wall.
One should lay down eight staffs (daṇḍas) as prescribed, according to the measurement of the base;
likewise, on that pedestal, [the divisions] are in fourth, fifth, and sixth parts.
One should appropriately fashion the staffs,
ropes, and so forth for the banners facing the temple, using the mantras of the respective guardians of the directions.
Having mounted [the deity] as before, the mantra-practitioner should then worship with perfumes and other offerings;
he should then present food colored according to the guardian of the direction, or pure food.
Then, having reached the sacrificial hall, one should perform the worship of the door and so forth;
having placed eight water-pots at the archways, starting from the east in due order.
One should worship Vighneśa, Bhārata, Śrī, Nandin, and Kāla upon the heads in the four directions; then, in the east, one should worship Bhṛṅgin and Vināyaka.

In the western [direction] are Vṛṣabha and Skanda; in the north are the goddesses Caṇḍā and [Pracaṇḍā], addressed by their respective names in the dative case, preceded by the syllable *oṃ* and ending with *namaḥ*.
Then, one should worship [the deities] along with their respective attendants upon the branches of the archways;
thereafter, one should worship the two Nidhis as prescribed—Praśānta and Śiśira.
The two [deities] named Parjanya and Śoka, who grant life to the earth and immortality,
as well as those who bestow wealth and prosperity, are to be worshipped in the water-pots with the Praṇava and likewise with the Heart-mantra.
Having performed the threefold consciousness and removed the pavilion-tree,
one should enter by way of the first of the five paths, preceded by the left foot.
Proceeding in a clockwise direction, he stood to the south of the lotus mandala;
facing north, he gazed auspiciously at the sacrificial materials.
Seated upon the auspicious throne, composed through the vision of reality,
he cast off his natural body and attained the state of Śiva by means of the Śambaras.
Having sacrificed, having offered oblations, and having established Śiva within the bindus,
one should make him the recipient by means of those substances and perform the ritual with the hand of action.
Then, having gathered the vardhanīs, and having established the base for the vardhanī in the northeast,
I shall sprinkle the sacrificial pavilion with perfumes, arghya water, and pure water.
Having placed the pitcher for Śiva’s arghya upon a heap of scattered grains on a sacrificial mound in the northeast,
the preceptor should also place the vardhanī vessel in the western direction.
One should worship the water-seat of the jar with the ritual thread, its tuft, along with fruits and sprouts, as well as gold and flowers.
One should worship the image of the deity and the sword with mantras, perfumes, and other offerings;
one should then place the Pāśupata weapon upon the Vardhanī vessel situated on a lion-throne.
[He should worship] Indra and the other world-protectors together with their weapons, stationed within the jars;
and having taken the *vardhanī* vessel, he should follow the gentle [deity] into the eight jars.
One should circumambulate the Śiva-kumbha, joined with the stream from the Vardhanī vessel,
while proclaiming the command of Śiva to the world-protectors for the protection of the sacrifice.
Having established the *kuṇḍa* and the *vardhanī*, one should worship the Lord Sthirādasa.
Thereafter, one should worship the *vardhanī* upon the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) on top of the altar (*vedikā*).
The *argha* offering should be prepared with pure *śāli* rice, those respective leaves made bitter, parched grain (*lāja*), and *darbha* grass; this bestows the increase of the five [senses].
One should properly draw a lotus at the end of the *tatva*;
one should place the jar named Śiva in the center, and likewise the *vardhanī*.
To the north, one should arrange the vessels for the Lords of Knowledge (Vidyeśvaras),
complete with their neck-threads, covered lids, and inner tufts of grass.
One should place the Śiva-kumbha and other vessels in sequence, with a capacity of one *droṇa* each;
nine gems in the vessel named after Śiva, and five gems in the *vardhanī*.
In the absence of the five jewels, one should place gold in the *vardhanī* vessel;
likewise, one should arrange golden flowers in the jars of the *Vidyeśvaras*.
One should place gems, gold, and flowers upon the Śiva-pitcher (śivaghaṭa);
a pair of garments upon the pitcher called Śiva; and a single garment upon the Vardhanī.
Having thus prepared everything, one should worship the Lord of Gods.
It was provided with special ablutions, endowed with exceptional ritual care,
accompanied by abundant sacrificial offerings, and furnished with betel leaves and other such items.
Then, for the sake of an extensive sacrifice to Soma, Skanda, Īśvara, and others,
he should perform the auspicious rite (*kautuka*) after being provided with a special ceremonial bath.
Then, having entered the pavilion, one should worship the Lord Śiva together with the Lord of Devas [the consort],
as well as the Śiva-vessel (śivakumbha), the deity, and the ritual implement (sādhana) along with its image.
One should worship the goddess Manonmanī together with her limbs (aṅgas) and perform the Vardhanī-nyāsa;
one should also worship the Vidyeśvaras as prescribed in the jars at the end of the night.
One should worship the Guru as he worships the mirror and other surfaces, the sun, water, and so forth, with Lakṣmī, Sarasvatī, and the Moon.
Having consecrated the fire-pit and other elements as before, one should prepare the Śiva-fire with mantras;
having divided it ninefold or fivefold, it should be placed in its respective directions within its own fire-pit.
In the middle portion of that [mandala], the Guru should satisfy Agni and Śiva along with his limbs (attendants) with the previously mentioned substances,
one hundred and eight times.
The guardians of the forms (mūrtipās) should offer oblations with their respective mantras and with the *śivāṇvardha* mantra;
at the end, however, they should offer the full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) as well as betel leaves and other such items.
At the conclusion of the fire-oblation, or at its beginning, the wise practitioner should offer the bali-offering,
which includes all [the ritual elements], accompanied by dance and adorned with every ornament.

One should perform the recitation of mantras from the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas, as well as the recitation of hymns, in the four directions; thereafter, one should offer the internal oblation (antarbali).
One should offer sandalwood and betel-leaves to the people, beginning with the preceptor;
at the conclusion of that, there shall be the offering of bali, the procedure for which is stated here.
One should fashion a linga made of fresh rice and consisting of sacrificial oblation mixed with curd;
as before, one should worship that primary image, along with its arms and wings, with perfumes and flowers.
One should worship [the deity] within other lingas, such as those of the world-protectors (lokapāla) and others;
therein, [one should visualize the deity] joined with the trident and endowed with the ten weapons.
One should offer the bali-oblation to the retinue beginning with Vṛṣa up until the banner (dhvaja),
while entering the city and other such places, in the location designated for the worship of the deities.
The preceptor and the disciple alike should offer the bali-oblation in due order;
on the first day, they should perform the worship of the Lord of the Gaṇas (Gaṇeśvara) with offerings such as jaggery, cakes, and edible foods.
On the second day, milk-rice and lotus flowers are dear to Brahmā;
on the third, however, one should offer an oblation of *kṛsara* rice with ghee to the spirits (*bhūtas*).
On the fourth night, there is powdered food mixed with ghee for the Gandharvas;
on the fifth day, that which is dear [to them] is offered with clarified butter for the sake of pleasing Indra.
On the sixth day, bamboo-grain food with curd is for the sages;
on the sixth day, rice mixed with jaggery and ghee is for the sages.
Let him offer [the oblation] on the seventh day...
on the eighth day, however, [he should offer] black gram food mixed with ghee for the Rākṣasas.
On the ninth day for Śiva, one should offer a bali-oblation consisting of pure food mixed with curd at the Brahma-sthāna.
A bali offering of pure food should be made for all the day-deities;
thereafter, for the sake of satisfying the Lords of the World, pure food mixed with curd should be offered.
Having entered the temple, one should offer the bali-oblation with one's own mantra;
[placing] the bali-stand... [upon] the sarvānna-liṅga.
In seven days, or five days, or three days, or on the night of the sky (the seventh day),
it should be performed as before with the image of the deity, accompanied by abundant lamps.
Adorned with all the aforementioned ornaments and endowed with every auspiciousness,
having thus performed the circumambulation, he entered the pavilion of the assembly hall.
Having performed the sequence of serving food as is appropriate,
and having offered water for the feet and other items, one should cause incense, a lamp, and sacred ash to be given.
Thus, every day at evening and at dawn, one should perform the ritual sequence;
beginning from the second day, this may also be done in the intervals between morning and evening.
One should especially construct the vehicles for the gods, beginning with Tripuraghna;
having performed the tying of the auspicious thread (kautuka-bandhana) for them on the preceding night.
At the end of the vehicle, a ceremonial bath should be performed; having offered the oblation, one should cause the moon-crested Lord to enter for the festival beginning from the third day.
Beginning from the fourth day, the festival of Umāskanda shall take place;
beginning from the fifth day, one should then worship Vṛṣeśvara.
Beginning from the sixth day, one should likewise [worship] Ardhanārīśvara;
during the first part of the night, [one should worship] the marriage-thread (kautuka) and all the deities.
In the fourth, fifth, and sixth [sections], one should especially smear [the ground] with a paste of saffron, agallochum, and sandalwood, respectively.
Having adorned the Lord of Gods and prepared the vehicle with oil, one should perform the rite;
on the evening of the seventh day, one should perform the oil massage.
p.
64) One should place rice before the deity and pour oil upon it;
having sprinkled it with the *arghya* water, one obtains [the fruit] through that mantra and the *saṃhitā-manu*.
Having veiled [the deity] with the three subtle threads, one should worship with scents and other offerings while reciting the heart-mantra (hṛdaya).
Then, having offered a tooth-stick and betel-leaf, one should perform the rite of showing [the deity] while reciting the heart-mantra.
The Guru, having uttered the wrathful mantra, should cause the oil to be given by means of the *śivānu* mantra;
he should likewise cause the tooth-stick and other items for the deities and others to be given in their proper sequence.
One should cause Nandin, Caṇḍeśvara, and the others to receive their offerings individually,
beginning with the Guru, accompanied by oil and betel.
Having performed the bathing and other rites for the Lord of the Gods,
one should bring him back at the conclusion of each [rite] to the sacrificial pavilion (yāgamaṇḍapa) for the ritual preparation (kalpita).
Having bathed and fully worshipped the deity, one should lead him for a pleasant sight;
having performed the circumambulation of the village, one should worship [the deity] at the temple.
On the eighth day, he should lead the Lord of Gods on a hunting expedition,
accompanied by elephants and horses, and engaged in the activities of commencing battle.
Furthermore, accompanied by Caṇḍeśvara, he should undertake a hunting expedition;
at the conclusion of the hunting expedition, however, [he should worship] the God with ritual bathing and other rites.
Having again performed the evening rites according to the previously mentioned procedure,
the wise practitioner should bathe the Lord of Dance that very night as well.
Having specially adorned the deity with white garments and other offerings,
and having presented incense, lamps, and so forth, one should then tie the protective thread (kautuka).
65) There, according to the previously mentioned procedure, one should offer an abundance of sacrificial oblations accompanied by all auspicious items and provided with cakes and other such foods.
Having placed [the image] upon a palanquin adorned with all ornaments and provided with various lamps,
one should lead it in a clockwise circumambulation.
There, in the assembly pavilion, one should pass the night with dances and other festivities;
then at dawn, the preceptor shall perform the ritual of offering the arghya and perfumes to Nṛtteśa.
One thousand, or half of that, or one hundred and eight;
or fifty less by one, or twenty-five.
All rites beginning with the installation of the sacred fire (agnyādhāna) should be performed according to the path prescribed for the fire-ritual (agnikārya);
however, at the conclusion, one should offer the expiatory oblation (prāyaścitta-homa) according to the rule and perform the worshipful offering (pūjyāhuti).
Thereafter, one should bathe the jar, and then cover it with a supreme cloth,
adorned with various ornaments and endowed with diverse garlands.
Then, having adorned it, one should offer incense, food offerings (naivedya), and so forth;
having prepared a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) beside that, one should place the vessel, the fire, and yakṣakardama [ointment].
One should place camphor and other substances upon the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila);
having sprinkled it with the weapon-mantra (hetimantra) and consecrated it, one should apply them while reciting the saṃhitā-mantras.
Having worshipped with perfumes and other offerings using the *hṛdaya* mantra, one should not obstruct [the ritual] with the *kavaca* mantra.
Then, in front of that, the Guru should prepare a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) and duly establish the *śivāgni*.
Having offered oblations of fuel-sticks, clarified butter, and cooked rice with the root mantra one hundred times,
there should then be an offering to the limbs (aṅga) by means of a portion of that same [mantra].
At the conclusion, one should perform the *pūrṇāhuti* and dismiss the fire of Śiva.
Having placed that [fire] within the vessel, one should establish it in Nṛtteśa by means of the root mantra.
Having smeared the limbs [of the images] with the substances as prescribed, the Guru should cause the goddesses to be offered [these offerings];
thereafter, he should cause the yakṣakardama paste to be given to the devotees.
One should give a cow with its calf, gold, rice, salt, sesame seeds,
clarified butter, and oil in due order, so as to satisfy the preceptor.
The gift accompanied by the offering of water is known as *yātrādāna*;
it should be endowed with all ornaments and provided with a face.
Having placed [the image] together with the presiding preceptor upon an excellent palanquin,
one should perform a circumambulation either within the fivefold enclosure or outside of it.
Having performed the prescribed sequence of the vehicle, which is endowed with the appropriate auspicious rites,
one should subsequently enter the pavilion and proceed with the sequence of the circumambulation.
Then, having offered water for the feet (*pādya*) and so forth, accompanied by [mantras] beginning with *oṃ*,
and having given coconut water and the like, one should again offer water for sipping (*ācamana*).
Then, having scattered durva grass, flowers, unbroken rice grains, and so forth in front, and having offered incense, lamps, and other offerings, together with all types of ornaments;
Then, having bathed Śiva with water containing playful ornaments,
one should remove the marriage-thread (kautuka) and present it to the Guru.
Having performed a special ablution and worshipped [the deity] with perfumes and other offerings,
one should cause betel-leaf mixed with abundant sacrificial food (havis) to be presented.
One should perform [the rite] at the time of evening twilight, having especially adorned the deity.
One should place the vehicle on that spot to the east, near the tooth-relic;
then one should perform the lustration ceremony as before, together with auspicious rites.
Having placed them there at night, one should cause them to enter the residence;
likewise, the kitchen and the sacrificial pavilion should be well-decorated.
Having offered [the oblation] to the deity right there with parched grains (lāja), one should always cause the water for the feet (pādya) and the sacrificial ashes (homa-bhūti) to be given.
Then, O twice-born one, having entered the sanctifying chamber (ghna), one should subsequently perform the bathing and other rites in due order.
On that night, having gone to a body of water in this manner before the rising of the sun on that day,
the Guru [should proceed].
O Goddess Gaṅgā, Yamunā, Narmadā, and Sarasvatī;
O Sindhu, Godāvarī, and you, Kāverī—may your presence be here.
Thus,
for the purification of sins, those who have been initiated should, during the interval between the rising and setting of the sun, recollect the Śiva-mantra behind the trident.
The best of preceptors should perform the *vācyatuka* rite at the sacred site;
then, on the tenth day, at the conclusion of the fire-oblation (*homa*), he should conduct the powder festival (*cūrṇotsava*).
Having taken cow-dung for smearing, one should prepare two altars (sthaṇḍila) before it;
on one place one should set down a trident (śūla), and on the other a mortar (ulūkhalu) and pestle (musala).
Having placed dūrvā grass, unbroken rice, oil, and plenty of betel leaf,
one should then immediately cast the powder of the night (rātricūrṇa) into the mortar.
One should worship the Lord of the Gods with water for the feet and other offerings, accompanied by incense;
one should perform the offering upon his head with sprouts of *dūrvā* grass, unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*), and so forth.
Or the Self is first from the Śiva-tattva, or else from the [subsequent] tattvas;
or again, he is the mouth of the Goddess, as well as the trident in its respective order.
One should worship the seed-syllable known as Ādhāra in sequence upon the pestle and the mortar;
the preceptor and others should perform the principal rite with dūrvā grass upon those two.
Then, with a sword, one should gradually crush the night-soil into three parts;
having taken that powder with the Astra-mantra, it should be infused into various vessels.

For the sake of the Liṅga and the Bera, for the trident, and for the people, one should procure oil separately in vessels for the sake of the Liṅga and the Bera, as well as for the jars and other items.
Having worshipped with the heart-mantra on the day of sprinkling and so forth, one should offer [the gift] preceded by betel-leaf;
and at night, powdered [substance] should be offered together with a trident.
One should quickly organize a powder festival (cūrṇotsava) with attendants following the bridegroom;
one should cause oil and betel to be distributed to the people, beginning with the elders.
Then, for the sake of a great pilgrimage site, one should bring [the image] to the ocean, a river, or similar location;
it should be joined with a drum and a trident, and adorned with all ornaments.
Then, one should prepare two sacrificial altars (*sthaṇḍila*) on the bank using rice and other materials;
having established a trident (*triśūla*) upon one, one may or may not place a water-pot (*kalaśa*) elsewhere.
Having provided them with thread-brushes (sūtrakūrca), cloth, and so forth, along with sprouts,
and having caused the declaration of an auspicious day (puṇyāha) to be recited, one should worship them with perfumes and other offerings.

Having summoned the deities, one should dispel the previously mentioned defects of the thread. Then, having released the *kautuka* (protective cord), one should bathe the trident with those same substances.
Then, as before, one should perform the immersion in the midst of the sacred bathing place (tīrtha);
having offered the water-trident-form upon the bank, one should proceed.
Having worshipped the trident, one should then install it in its abode.
Those best of men who perform the ritual bath with the trident [attain great merit].
They too go to the abode of Śiva, and for them there shall be no further rebirth;
having reached the sacrificial pavilion, one should then perform the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti).
Then, at the time of midday, the preceptor, having worshipped the deity and brought the sacrificial jar situated for the rite, which is endowed with all auspicious things, [should proceed].
Having led [the deity] around the liṅga-base in due order by way of circumambulation,
one should place the God, the Goddess, and the Lords of Knowledge (vidyeśas) all around, starting from the northeast.
Thereafter, one should perform worship according to the extent of one's means.
In the evening, one should lead [the image] later for the sake of the supreme pilgrimage site;
at night, there is the descent of the world-protectors (*lokapāla*).

Having performed this, one should maintain the sequence of serving [the offerings] starting from that day for seven days, accompanied by all musical instruments and the like, without any deficiency in the vehicles.
After seven days of silence, it should be accompanied by a sacrifice;
at its conclusion, there shall be worship of Caṇḍa, joined with fire-oblations and hymns of praise.
Having first led Caṇḍeśvara [in procession], one should perform the *yāna* for seven days.
(The seven-day rite should be accompanied by all musical instruments and the like, or it may be performed without the *yāna*.)
At its end, one should lead forth the sacred ford (tīrtha) as before, together with the trident.
On that night, one should perform the hoisting of the banner according to the prescribed ritual;
this is declared to be the festival known as Vijayā, which is especially observed on these [specified] days.
One should perform all the rites for the ancestors, such as those lasting fifteen days and so forth, as prescribed by Vijaya;
likewise, one should worship the eight world-protectors and the banner, while excluding the *bhaktaliṅga*.
O Goddess, one should perform the *koddiṣṭa* rites for the ancestors;
for at the sacred site (*tīrtha*) in the temple of the deity, the festival of the banner (*dhvaja*) occurs by day and by night.
In descending order, for those aged fifty-four, eleven, eleven, and eleven,
or for those with ten thousand, fifteen thousand, or ten thousand [units], the penance is prescribed beyond that.
On the constellation Dhvajāvaroha, one should perform the ceremonial bathing (snapana) with those [deities] known as Śuddha;
this applies to the Linga, the image (bera), the bull (vṛṣa), and the trident (śūla), according to the method prescribed for bathing.
Having worshipped him thoroughly as prescribed for the rite of worship, one should adorn him with garlands;
and at night, one should worship Caṇḍeśvara along with the ritual ablution.
Having offered the gift of purification (vadyaka) along with the fire-oblation (homa), [one should acknowledge]:
"Whatever has been done by me, whether intentionally or unintentionally, that was deficient or excessive."
Then, O Caṇḍanātha, by your command, the Guru should go to the base of the banner and other locations filled with vital points (marmas), and subsequently perform the fire sacrifice (homa).
One should release the bull for the sake of the hundred oblations with the *ṛṣabha* mantra;
then, having released the bull, one should cause the four horses to run.
Then one should offer the village-oblation (*grāmabali*), provided with food and a linga,
accompanied by a trident and all the sounds of musical instruments.
At the time of offering the bali, one should sound all musical instruments;
otherwise, maintaining silence, one should perform the bali known as "mauna."
Having entered the village and offered the bali-oblation to Brahmā and the other deities, one should dismiss them;
then, having entered the house, one should cast the bali upon the bali-pīṭha.
At the beginning of a festival, in its midst, and at its conclusion, there should be a celebration for the devotees;
indeed, that very celebration must be performed according to one's ability.
Having performed the festival for the sake of monthly worship on Mount Damanaka or Rohaṇa and so forth—
after first tying the auspicious thread (kautuka) either at night or even during the day with musical instruments— ...
The teacher should be honored with garments, gold, and finger-rings;
the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) should consist of fifteen niṣkas as a minimum, increasing according to one's means.
The best of men should cause whatever materials were used for the sacrifice to be given to the preceptor;
thus, he should perform the great festival with faith.
"Having uplifted three times seven generations of his lineage, he shall attain the state of Śiva.
Thus ends the chapter on the Festival of Devotion in the *Vijaya-tantra*, within the *Tri-sahasra-saṃhitā*.
Thus ends the Vijayottara Tantra.
